 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'Sleep Interventions Designed to Improve Athletic Performance and Recovery: A Systematic Review of Current Approaches' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "PRISMA systematic review (PubMed, PsycINFO and Web of Science searched in 2016 and updated in 2017) of 10 sleep intervention studies with 218 competitive athletes aged 18 to 24 years from several sports. Sleep extension had the most beneficial effects on subsequent performance, while napping, sleep hygiene and post-exercise recovery strategies gave mixed results.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 10 studies were included, four had 15 or fewer participants, seven used male athletes only, and study quality was mostly moderate (one good, one poor). The athletes ranged from amateur to elite, and the review reports no pooled effect estimate, so the evidence is narrative.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read 'sleep extension improves performance' as an established athlete intervention, when it rests on a few small, mostly male studies and the authors call for further testing.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2018,
   "citation": "Bonnar D, Bartel K, Kakoschke N, Lang C. Sleep Interventions Designed to Improve Athletic Performance and Recovery: A Systematic Review of Current Approaches. Sports Med. 2018.",
   "doi": "10.1007/s40279-017-0832-x",
   "abstract": "This PRISMA systematic review identified 10 sleep intervention studies with 218 competitive athletes aged 18 to 24 years. Sleep extension had the most beneficial effects on subsequent performance, while napping, sleep hygiene and post-exercise recovery strategies gave mixed results, and the authors outline a structured athlete sleep program for future testing.",
   "tldr": "In the studies reviewed, sleep extension gave the clearest performance benefit for athletes, and napping, sleep hygiene and recovery strategies gave mixed results. The evidence base is small, so use these findings to shape individual sleep plans and not as a fixed protocol.",
   "methods": "Systematic search of PubMed, PsycINFO and Web of Science (May 2016, updated September 2017) following PRISMA guidelines. Ten studies were included if they tested a sleep intervention in competitive athletes and reported performance, recovery, sleepiness or fatigue outcomes, and each was rated on a modified 8-item quality scale.",
   "findings": "Sleep extension in basketball and tennis players improved outcomes such as sprint time, shooting and serving accuracy, reaction time and daytime sleepiness, with the basketball study using 5 to 7 weeks of extended sleep. Acute sleep hygiene increased sleep duration without improving later performance, and a one-month education program was linked to subjective soccer performance gains. Post-exercise recovery studies (whole-body cryostimulation and evening red light) improved sleep measures, with small performance changes in one study.",
   "limitations": "Only 10 studies with 218 athletes were reviewed, several with very small samples, and most used male athletes only. Quality ratings were mostly moderate, and the review reports no pooled effect size, so the strength of the conclusions is limited.",
   "practicalImplications": "For athletes with partial sleep restriction, increasing time in bed is the best-supported option in this review, with sleep diaries or actigraphy to check the effect. Sleep hygiene and recovery strategies can be introduced, but the evidence for performance gains from them is mixed.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance staff could prioritize extra time in bed for athletes with short sleep, and use a nap of about 2 hours after training when extended night sleep is not possible, as the authors suggest. The structured sleep program in the paper was not tested, so treat it as a proposal to pilot with your own squad.",
   "rtp": "This review does not inform return-to-sport decisions, because the included studies used healthy competitive athletes and did not assess injured athletes or recovery from injury. It can support general sleep planning in healthy athletes only."
 }
}

    REVIEW ARTICLE



Sleep Monitoring in Athletes: Motivation, Methods, Miscalculations
and Why it Matters
Shona L. Halson1


© Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2019


Abstract
It is increasingly recognised that many athletes have poor sleep quantity and/or quality despite the advances in knowledge
regarding the importance of sleep for an athletic population. The majority of research in sleep assessment and treatment
(within the general population) focuses on the medical disorder insomnia, and therefore may not be specifically relevant for
athletes. Further, there are currently no guidelines for the standardisation of assessment, intervention, feedback and behav-
iour change strategies in athletes. This review outlines potential reasons for sleep disturbances in athletes, advantages and
disadvantages of a range of methods to assess sleep (polysomnography, activity monitoring, consumer sleep technology,
sleep diaries and questionnaires), considerations for the provision of feedback, a description of potential interventions and
behaviour change challenges and strategies. The objective of this review is to provide practitioners with the latest scientific
evidence in an area rapidly progressing in awareness, consumerism and athlete engagement.

 "screeningLimitations": "No systematic search method is described, so study selection and the strength of the recommendations cannot be checked. Several validation studies cited are small and based on team-sport or semi-professional samples, and the review itself notes that some devices have no published validation.",

   "abstract": "This review outlines reasons for sleep disturbance in athletes, the advantages and disadvantages of methods to assess sleep (polysomnography, activity monitoring, consumer sleep technology, sleep diaries and questionnaires), considerations for feedback, and intervention and behaviour change strategies. It is written to give practitioners current evidence in an area where monitoring is growing faster than standards.",
   "tldr": "Athlete sleep monitoring needs validated tools, careful interpretation and supportive feedback. Research-grade actigraphy with a sleep diary is the most defensible option in this review, while consumer wearables and apps are better used to start conversations than to make decisions.",
   "methods": "Narrative review of the literature on sleep assessment in athletes. It describes each monitoring tool with its advantages and disadvantages, a suggested monitoring process, and a worked case of one Olympic athlete monitored with a 14-day actigraphy and diary period.",
   "findings": "Research-grade activity monitors agreed with polysomnography in athletes (81 to 90% agreement, 81 to 92% sensitivity), but their accuracy depends on the scoring threshold. In one study of 12 semi-professional soccer players, a consumer wearable's mean total sleep time difference from polysomnography was 51.5 min (SD 152.4) with very wide limits, and a popular sleep app showed no correlation with polysomnography for sleep efficiency. In one rugby league study, education and monitoring improved sleep only during the education period.",
   "limitations": "The review has no described systematic search, and its conclusions rest partly on small validation studies. The author notes that there are currently no published validation studies of some popular wearables, and that there are no standard monitoring procedures or guidelines for athletes.",
   "practicalImplications": "A practical approach is a 1 to 2 week actigraphy period with a sleep diary during a training cycle, with referral to a sleep physician if a sleep disorder is suspected. Consumer device and app data should be used as a starting point for discussion, and feedback should focus on what can be improved rather than on poor scores.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance staff could use a 14-day actigraphy and diary period during a training block to find routine problems such as inconsistent bed and wake times, as the case study does. Feedback should focus on the aspects that can be changed, and wearable sleep scores should not drive training decisions until they are validated.",
   "rtp": "The review does not address return-to-sport timing or injured athletes. Its only point relevant to rehabilitation staff is that a suspected sleep disorder should be investigated and referred to a sleep physician as a priority."

24	                                         Sleep is a fundamental biological process in athletes, indispensable for tissue regeneration,
25	                                         exercise adaptation, and injury prevention. Disruptions in sleep architecture and duration
26	                                         have been consistently associated with diminished physical performance and adverse
27	                                         health outcomes, impairing muscular strength, power output, and endurance capacity, and
28	                                         concurrently compromising cognitive function. On a physiological level, insufficient sleep
29	                                         disrupts endocrine homeostasis, elevating cortisol levels and reducing anabolic hormones
30	Academic Editors: Michele Roccella
31	and Ana Adan                             such as testosterone and growth hormone. At the molecular level, sleep loss promotes the
32	                                         upregulation of pro-apoptotic gene expression and exacerbates pro-inflammatory signalling
33	Received: 27 August 2025
34	Revised: 16 September 2025               pathways. Optimal sleep duration and quality represent a critical “regenerative window”,
35	Accepted: 22 October 2025                essential for enhancing athletic performance and safeguarding physiological resilience.
36	Published: 27 October 2025               Ensuring adequate sleep among athletes can be effectively achieved through educational,
37	Citation: Kaczmarek, F.;                 behavioural, and nutritional interventions outlined in this review.
38	Bartkowiak-Wieczorek, J.; Matecka,
39	M.; Jenczylik, K.; Brzezińska, K.;      Keywords: physiology of sleep; sleep disorders; sleep quality; sleep architecture; sleep
40	Gajniak, P.; Marchwiak, S.; Kaczmarek,   deprivation; circadian rhythms; athletic performance; regeneration
41	K.; Nowak, M.; Kmiecik, M.; et al.
42	Sleep and Athletic Performance: A
43	Multidimensional Review of
44	Physiological and Molecular
45	Mechanisms. J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14,
46	                                         1. Introduction
47	7606. https://doi.org/10.3390/                Sleep is a fundamental biological process for maintaining the integrity and adaptability
48	jcm14217606                              of the organism. Adults typically sleep an average of 7–8 h per day, which constitutes
49	Copyright: © 2025 by the authors.        approximately one-third of their lives, underscoring its crucial role in maintaining home-
50	Licensee MDPI, Basel, Switzerland.       ostasis. However, there are significant differences in sleep duration between genders,
51	This article is an open access article   geographic regions, and age groups [1]. Further, qualitative and quantitative sleep distur-
52	distributed under the terms and
53	                                         bances are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular, metabolic, and psychiatric
54	conditions of the Creative Commons
55	                                         disorders [2].
56	Attribution (CC BY) license
57	(https://creativecommons.org/                 For athletes, sleep takes on special importance as a key element of regeneration,
58	licenses/by/4.0/).                       exercise adaptation, and injury prevention. During sleep, a range of physiological processes
59	
60	
61	J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                  https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm14217606
62	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                            2 of 43
63	
64	
65	
66	                               occur that support tissue repair and energy resource replenishment [3] as well as anti-
67	                               inflammatory mediators [2].
68	                                     Sleep architecture also provides optimal conditions for hormonal, neurological, and
69	                               anabolic processes [4]. Sleep is not merely passive rest but a highly active and complex
70	                               biological process during which the body carries out mechanisms essential for health
71	                               and performance [1]. On a hormonal level, sleep regulates the balance between anabolic
72	                               and catabolic hormones. During deep sleep (N3), there is a surge in growth hormone,
73	                               testosterone, and IGF-1 secretion—hormones crucial for tissue repair, protein synthesis,
74	                               and muscle growth. Even a single night without sleep can reduce testosterone levels by
75	                               nearly one-quarter, while chronic sleep deprivation promotes catabolic dominance. At
76	                               the same time, insufficient sleep disrupts cortisol regulation; in excess, cortisol accelerates
77	                               protein breakdown and hinders recovery [4].
78	                                     The brain also works actively during sleep to organise and process information. In
79	                               NREM stage 2, procedural memory consolidation occurs, strengthening motor skills and
80	                               athletic techniques. REM sleep, on the other hand, promotes the creation of new strategies
81	                               and integration of information into broader patterns, enhancing creativity and tactical
82	                               thinking. According to the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis, sleep allows the weakening
83	                               of less relevant neural connections, creating space for new ones and maintaining learning
84	                               capacity. Conversely, sleep deprivation reduces focus, slows reaction time, impairs decision-
85	                               making, and weakens motor coordination—factors critical in sports performance. In
86	                               addition, inadequate sleep promotes the accumulation of neurotoxic β-amyloid, further
87	                               impairing brain function [1–4].
88	                                     On a somatic level, sleep is the body’s most important recovery window. During deep
89	                               sleep, muscle repair and protein synthesis intensify, and energy stores, including muscle
90	                               glycogen, are replenished. Extended sleep deprivation significantly reduces the ability to
91	                               restore glycogen, directly lowering endurance and limiting the capacity for high-intensity
92	                               exercise [3]. Sleep also regulates the immune system—supporting anti-inflammatory
93	                               cytokine activity—while its deficiency raises levels of inflammatory markers such as IL-6
94	                               and CRP, which hinder tissue repair and delay the return to peak performance [2].
95	                                     Insufficient sleep leads to declines in strength, power, endurance, and cognitive func-
96	                               tion and is also linked to higher rates of injury in young athletes. Additionally, inadequate
97	                               sleep negatively affects mental health and regenerative capacity [5].
98	                                     At the cellular level, sleep modulates the immune and hormonal systems, as well
99	                               as inflammatory cytokines—all of which are crucial for post-exercise regeneration and
100	                               adaptation [4]. Recent evidence also indicates the involvement of epigenetic mechanisms
101	                               (e.g., DNA methylation and microRNAs) in the regulation of adaptive processes at the
102	                               molecular level [6]. As a result, high-quality and adequate sleep duration serves as a natural
103	                               “regeneration window”, supporting performance growth, health protection, oxidative stress
104	                               reduction, and improved training adaptation [7].
105	                                     Frequent and prolonged travelling—often involving transitioning across time zones—
106	                               is inherent in the lifestyle of professional athletes and presents negative consequences,
107	                               including disruptions to the circadian rhythm, resulting in both reduced sleep quantity
108	                               and quality. Sleep disturbances may also manifest in less conventional ways, includ-
109	                               ing gastrointestinal dysfunction, impaired cognitive and executive functioning, memory
110	                               deficits, and emotional dysregulation. Collectively, these factors compromise recovery and
111	                               athletic performance.
112	                                     We provide a comprehensive overview of the role of sleep in sport, with particular
113	                               emphasis on its regenerative functions and underlying physiological, molecular, and epige-
114	                               netic mechanisms. Selected sleep disorders and their assessment methods are discussed,
115	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                        3 of 43
116	
117	
118	
119	                               aiming to present sleep not only as a passive state of rest but as a dynamic and essential
120	                               contributor to athletic performance, overall health, and injury prevention.
121	
122	                               2. Methodology
123	                                    A narrative review was conducted using the PubMed/Medline and Cochrane
124	                               databases. The following English terms and their combinations were used: athletes,
125	                               sleep, sleep deprivation, sleep loss, sleep disorders, insomnia, exercise, sport, perfor-
126	                               mance, nap, physiology, pathophysiology, anxiety, stress, treatment, pharmacological, and
127	                               non-pharmacological.
128	                                    The search process was conducted stepwise. Initially, broad queries were applied,
129	                               such as “athletes AND sleep” (7728 results, including 3945 articles published in the last
130	                               five years), followed by more specific combinations targeting physiological and thera-
131	                               peutic aspects and focusing on studies published in the last five years. For example:
132	                               “athletes AND sleep AND physiology” (1259 results), “athletes AND sleep AND sleep
133	                               deprivation” (190 results), and “athletes AND sleep AND stress” (694 results). Additional
134	                               queries addressed treatment approaches, including pharmacological (157 results) and
135	                               non-pharmacological (36 results).
136	                                    Approximately 7700 publications were identified. After screening the titles and ab-
137	                               stracts, 178 articles were selected for evaluation. Each manuscript was then critically
138	                               assessed and classified into two main groups: review articles and experimental studies.
139	                               Subsequently, reference lists of the most relevant works were also analysed, leading to the
140	                               inclusion of additional papers.
141	                                    We excluded studies exclusively addressing psychological interventions, research
142	                               involving children or older adults, and papers not directly related to sleep in athletes.
143	                               Given the breadth of the subject, a selective choice of factors affecting sleep was made.
144	                               The final selection focused on literature concerning the physiology of sleep, the bidirec-
145	                               tional relationship between sleep and physical activity, the influence of diet and stress,
146	                               sleep disorders, pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments, as well as sleep
147	                               assessment tools.
148	                                    We present a simple Flow Diagram (Scheme 1) illustrating the process of literature
149	                               identification, screening, and inclusion.
150	
151	
152	
153	
154	                               Scheme 1. FLOW DIAGRAM illustrating the process of literature identification, screening
155	                               and inclusion.
156	
157	                               3. The Physiology of Sleep
158	                                    Sleep constitutes a fundamental psychophysiological process indispensable for pre-
159	                               serving physiological capacity, health, and overall well-being, especially within athletic
160	                               populations. Sleep and athletic performance remain in a close, bidirectional relationship.
161	                               On the one hand, adequate sleep duration and quality form the foundation of recovery,
162	                               supporting muscle repair, hormonal regulation, and cognitive processes that underlie
163	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                               4 of 43
164	
165	
166	
167	                               decision-making and motor coordination [1–4]. Even short-term sleep deprivation leads to
168	                               reduced strength, power, and endurance, impaired reaction time, as well as disturbances
169	                               in cognitive functions—all factors that determine athletic outcomes. Chronic sleep de-
170	                               ficiency exacerbates catabolic processes through elevated cortisol levels and decreased
171	                               testosterone and growth hormone concentrations, thereby limiting protein synthesis and
172	                               muscle recovery capacity [4].
173	                                    On the other hand, physical activity itself and high training intensity influence sleep.
174	                               Moderate exercise can improve sleep depth and facilitate recovery, whereas excessive
175	                               training loads, pre-competition stress, or frequent travel across time zones may lead to
176	                               circadian rhythm disruptions, difficulties falling asleep, and sleep fragmentation [1–4]. In
177	                               young athletes, insufficient sleep increases the risk of musculoskeletal injuries, while in
178	                               professional athletes, it reduces training efficiency and prolongs the time required to restore
179	                               peak performance [3,4].
180	                                    The literature emphasises that extending sleep duration (“sleep extension”) improves
181	                               technical precision, reaction time, shooting accuracy, and aerobic performance, while short
182	                               naps can partly compensate for nocturnal sleep deficits and support recovery [2–4]. Conse-
183	                               quently, sleep is considered a key “recovery window” for athletes, with its insufficiency
184	                               counteracting the benefits of even the most carefully designed training program [3,4].
185	                                    Sleep consists of two major phases: rapid eye movement (REM) and non-rapid eye
186	                               movement (NREM) sleep. NREM is further divided into three distinct stages—N1, N2,
187	                               and N3—each characterised by specific brainwave patterns, eye movements, and levels
188	                               of muscle tone (Figure 1). During sleep, a healthy athlete can cycle through the sleep
189	                               stages approximately 4 to 6 times, with each full cycle lasting approximately 90 min. Many
190	                               factors influence the quality and structure of sleep, including age, mood disorders such as
191	                               depression, traumatic brain injuries, medications, sporting activity and circadian rhythm
192	                               disturbances. Detailed physiological processes involved in these changes are described
193	                               under the concept of “pathophysiology” [8].
194	                                    Human sleep is characterised by distinctive neural oscillations observable through an
195	                               electroencephalogram (EEG), which demonstrates the various functional stages of sleep.
196	                               During Stage N1, the transition from wakefulness is marked by the reduction in alpha
197	                               activity and the emergence of theta waves (4–7 Hz), often accompanied by vertex sharp
198	                               transients and slow eye movements. These low-frequency rhythms signal the brain to
199	                               move away from external awareness while drifting towards deeper rest [9].
200	
201	
202	
203	
204	                               Figure 1. Physiological stages of sleep. Figure inspired by Driller et al. (2023) [10]. Created in
205	                               BioRender. Kaczmarek, F. (2025) https://BioRender.com/heatk8t, (accessed on 20 October 2025).
206	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                         5 of 43
207	
208	
209	
210	                                     Within Stage N2, two hallmark waveforms appear: sleep spindles and K-complexes.
211	                               Sleep spindles consist of rhythmic bursts at 12–14 Hz lasting about 0.5–1.5 s, generated by
212	                               thalamocortical circuits. They act as sensory gatekeepers and play a key role in memory
213	                               consolidation, evidenced by increased spindle density correlating with better recall. K-
214	                               complexes are large, biphasic waves exceeding 100 µV, serving to protect sleep from
215	                               disruptions and aiding synaptic homeostasis. These too are linked to memory processes.
216	                               There is strong evidence confirming a correlation between the duration of stage 2 sleep
217	                               and the consolidation of motor memory. For athletes, sufficient time spent in stage 2 sleep
218	                               is crucial for the long-term retention of techniques and motor patterns, which directly
219	                               translates into subsequent performance [11].
220	                                     Stage N3, or slow-wave sleep, is defined by delta waves (0.5–4 Hz, >75 µV), which
221	                               reflect synchronised cortical activity facilitating physical and immune system restoration.
222	                               Importantly, sharp-wave ripples, the high-frequency oscillations originating in the hip-
223	                               pocampus, are tightly coupled with delta waves. These ripples mark moments when
224	                               memories are replayed and transferred from the hippocampus to the cortex for long-term
225	                               storage [12]. The deep sleep phase (N3) is particularly important, as this is when the
226	                               mechanisms enabling muscle recovery and protein synthesis are amplified. Studies have
227	                               demonstrated that insufficient slow-wave sleep disrupts growth hormone (GH) secretion
228	                               and alters cortisol levels, thereby impairing post-exercise muscle recovery. Moreover, re-
229	                               duced slow-wave activity promotes inflammatory processes, as sleep restriction elevates
230	                               pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, CRP), which hinder muscle tissue repair and delay the
231	                               restoration of optimal performance [4].
232	                                     During REM sleep, the EEG exhibits mixed, low-amplitude theta (4–8 Hz) and
233	                               beta/gamma (>30 Hz) activity together with REMs and muscle atonia. REM is further
234	                               characterised by sawtooth waves, ponto-geniculo-occipital (PGO) waves, and synchronised
235	                               theta–gamma oscillations. PGO waves, originating in the pons and propagating through
236	                               the lateral geniculate nucleus to the visual cortex, align closely with hippocampal theta,
237	                               supporting emotional memory processing and vivid dreaming. The coupling of theta phase
238	                               and gamma amplitude—especially in the hippocampus—is linked to enhanced memory
239	                               consolidation during REM [13] (Figure 2). In athletes, REM sleep facilitates the generation
240	                               of new strategies and enhances the assimilation of information by strengthening memory
241	                               traces associated with training.
242	                                     Sleep architecture provides essential conditions for hormonal regulation, anabolic
243	                               activity, and neurological processes. Although sleep may appear disadvantageous, because
244	                               it increases vulnerability to predators, limits food intake, and restricts opportunities for
245	                               reproduction, it persists throughout the animal kingdom. This persistence is likely ex-
246	                               plained by its crucial role in brain and behavioural development, as well as in memory
247	                               reorganisation [4]. Three main hypotheses have been proposed to explain the role of sleep
248	                               in the brain development of mammalian neonates. The Ontogenetic Hypothesis suggests
249	                               that the amount of sleep or phasic sleep activity is closely related to brain development
250	                               and maturation. According to the study by Frank, pharmacological deprivation of REM
251	                               sleep can cause abnormal brain development or behaviour [14]. The studies performed on
252	                               rodents have shown that it can cause changes in cholinergic and monoaminergic systems,
253	                               neurotransmission, and the survival of neurons [15].

262	                                     A second theory, the Consolidation Hypothesis, proposes that sleep provides a critical
263	                               window for consolidating experience. This process occurs primarily during developmental
264	                               periods of heightened, experience-dependent brain plasticity. The third explanation, the
265	                               Synaptic Homeostasis Hypothesis (SHY), states that sleep enables the reduction in the num-
266	                               ber of synapses, selectively weakening less important connections while preserving those
267	                               essential for transmitting critical information. This process makes room for the formation
268	                               of new synapses [14]. Tononi et al., in their study, describe sleep as “the price the brain
269	                               pays for its neuroplasticity”. Scientists agree with SHY and emphasise the role of normal
270	                               sleep architecture in synaptic and cellular homeostasis, which must align with the plastic
271	                               changes present during normal wakefulness. The balance of synaptic downscaling, learn-
272	                               ing processes, and synaptogenesis is necessary to prevent saturation of synaptic networks
273	                               and maintain neuroplasticity [16]. The study by Colavito et al. indicates that sleep depri-
274	                               vation, when performed correctly, results in memory dysfunction in rodents. Although
275	                               the study reports that sleep deprivation significantly impairs hippocampus-dependent
276	                               spatial memory consolidation and contextual fear memory, the cued fear memory appears
277	                               to remain unaffected by the loss of sleep, which shows that the effect of altered sleeping
278	                               affects various types of memory differently [17]. At the synaptic level, although the total
279	                               strength of connections underlying specific memories remains unknown, molecular, elec-
280	                               trophysiological, and structural markers indicate a reduction in synaptic strength in the
281	                               cerebral cortex and hippocampus. These findings are consistent with SHY, which proposes
282	                               that synaptic downscaling during sleep is balanced by the selective strengthening of con-
283	                               nections that support learning and memory reorganisation [18]. The duration and quality
284	                               of sleep influence not only the neurological processes, but also the activity of the endocrine
285	                               system. This is because concentrations of specific hormones, such as GH and cortisol,

291	                               and endocrine function. The study by Sassin et al. discovered that significant release of
292	                               GH occurs during slow-wave sleep during stages 3 and 4 [19]. Additionally, the cortisol
293	                               level rapidly grows about 30 min after awakening. This phenomenon is known as a cortisol
294	                               awakening response. Wright et al. studied the relationship between sleep deprivation,
295	                               circadian misalignment, and cortisol levels among other factors. In their study, they showed
296	                               that acute sleep deprivation increased cortisol levels during the evening and early morning
297	                               hours. On the other hand, chronic circadian misalignment decreased cortisol levels over
298	                               the 24-h day [20]. Adequate sleep duration is necessary to maintain proper hunger and
299	                               satiety. Spielberg et al. claimed that sleep restriction changed levels of appetite-related
300	                               hormones. In their study, two consecutive nights of restricted sleep (four hours in bed) in
301	                               young, healthy men resulted in a 24% increase in ghrelin (a hunger hormone) and an 18%
302	                               decrease in leptin (a hunger-suppressing hormone). Moreover, participants demonstrated
303	                               a stronger preference for calorie-dense foods rich in carbohydrates [21].

305	                               3.1. Neurochemical Mechanisms of Sleep and Wakefulness
306	                                     The inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) plays a crucial
307	                               role in initiating sleep by binding to GABA-A receptors in the brain [22]. Sleep-promoting
308	                               neurons in the anterior hypothalamus release GABA, which suppresses wake-promoting
309	                               regions in the hypothalamus and brainstem. GABA plays a central role in promoting
310	                               slow-wave sleep, thereby supporting athletes’ physical recovery, hormonal balance, and
311	                               muscle repair following intensive exercise. Adenosine also facilitates sleep by inhibiting
312	                               orexinergic neurons in the hypothalamus while activating neurons in the preoptic area.
313	                               Through its progressive accumulation during wakefulness, it promotes sleep pressure and
314	                               facilitates recovery processes, making it a critical factor in athletes’ restoration of physical
315	                               performance and prevention of overtraining [23,24].
316	                                     Conversely, neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine (ACh), dopamine, norepinephrine,
317	                               serotonin, histamine, and orexin peptides work together to maintain wakefulness. In ath-
318	                               letes, these mechanisms are particularly important, as effective activation of the arousal
319	                               system influences vigilance, reaction time, motor coordination, and physical performance.
320	                               Regular physical training can modulate the functioning of these neurochemical pathways,
321	                               leading to increased dopaminergic and noradrenergic activity and optimized orexin release,
322	                               which supports better regulation of circadian rhythms, energy levels, and adaptive capacity
323	                               to physical exertion. Acetylcholine release is highest during both wakefulness and REM
324	                               sleep, but significantly lower during NREM [23]. Serotonin is produced by neurons in the
325	                               raphe nuclei, norepinephrine by the locus coeruleus, and histamine by the tuberomam-
326	                               millary nucleus of the posterior hypothalamus. Orexin, synthesised in the hypothalamus,
327	                               communicates with key arousal centres to sustain alertness [24].
328	                                     Sleep is intertwined with the circadian rhythms that are linked to the daily rhythms
329	                               of temperature and light. Throughout evolution, this linkage became more nuanced, but
330	                               the basic rest-activity cycles still play a role in the life of organisms. Human sleep is a
331	                               result of a series of molecules that are released locally, and when their effects are summed,
332	                               they change the activity of the entire system [25]. These molecules play a significant role
333	                               in keeping us asleep and awake. The level of dopamine, an important neurotransmitter
334	                               that affects reward-motivated behaviour, increases during the night and is controlled by
335	                               the circadian rhythms. The decrease in serotonin (5-HT), which regulates emotions and
336	                               mental well-being, can disrupt the rest-activity cycle. Glutamate, on the other hand, sends
337	                               information about the presence of light from the retino-hypothalamic tract (RHT) to the
338	                               hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), which induces changes in sleep phases
339	                               and increases during the day. Norepinephrine, which modulates attention, arousal, and

345	                                       is a hormone produced by the pineal gland that regulates sleep onset and latency [26].
346	                                       All of those substances and many more play a significant role in the process of sleeping.
347	                                       In athletes, a balanced regulation of these neurotransmitters and hormones is crucial for
348	                                       efficient recovery, maintenance of physical performance, and adaptation to training loads.
349	                                       Adenosine triphosphate (ATP), adenosine, nitric oxide (NO), prostaglandins, interleukin-1β

                                         concurrently compromising cognitive function. On a physiological level, insufficient sleep
                                         disrupts endocrine homeostasis, elevating cortisol levels and reducing anabolic hormones

J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                  https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm14217606

                               occur that support tissue repair and energy resource replenishment [3] as well as anti-
                               inflammatory mediators [2].
                                     Sleep architecture also provides optimal conditions for hormonal, neurological, and
                               anabolic processes [4]. Sleep is not merely passive rest but a highly active and complex
                               biological process during which the body carries out mechanisms essential for health
                               and performance [1]. On a hormonal level, sleep regulates the balance between anabolic
                               and catabolic hormones. During deep sleep (N3), there is a surge in growth hormone,
                               testosterone, and IGF-1 secretion—hormones crucial for tissue repair, protein synthesis,
                               and muscle growth. Even a single night without sleep can reduce testosterone levels by
                               nearly one-quarter, while chronic sleep deprivation promotes catabolic dominance. At
                               the same time, insufficient sleep disrupts cortisol regulation; in excess, cortisol accelerates
                               protein breakdown and hinders recovery [4].
                                     The brain also works actively during sleep to organise and process information. In
                               NREM stage 2, procedural memory consolidation occurs, strengthening motor skills and
                               athletic techniques. REM sleep, on the other hand, promotes the creation of new strategies
                               and integration of information into broader patterns, enhancing creativity and tactical
                               thinking. According to the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis, sleep allows the weakening
                               of less relevant neural connections, creating space for new ones and maintaining learning
                               capacity. Conversely, sleep deprivation reduces focus, slows reaction time, impairs decision-
                               making, and weakens motor coordination—factors critical in sports performance. In
                               addition, inadequate sleep promotes the accumulation of neurotoxic β-amyloid, further
                               impairing brain function [1–4].
                                     On a somatic level, sleep is the body’s most important recovery window. During deep
                               sleep, muscle repair and protein synthesis intensify, and energy stores, including muscle
                               glycogen, are replenished. Extended sleep deprivation significantly reduces the ability to
                               restore glycogen, directly lowering endurance and limiting the capacity for high-intensity
                               exercise [3]. Sleep also regulates the immune system—supporting anti-inflammatory
                               cytokine activity—while its deficiency raises levels of inflammatory markers such as IL-6
                               and CRP, which hinder tissue repair and delay the return to peak performance [2].
                                     Insufficient sleep leads to declines in strength, power, endurance, and cognitive func-
                               tion and is also linked to higher rates of injury in young athletes. Additionally, inadequate
                               sleep negatively affects mental health and regenerative capacity [5].
                                     At the cellular level, sleep modulates the immune and hormonal systems, as well
                               as inflammatory cytokines—all of which are crucial for post-exercise regeneration and
                               adaptation [4]. Recent evidence also indicates the involvement of epigenetic mechanisms
                               (e.g., DNA methylation and microRNAs) in the regulation of adaptive processes at the
                               molecular level [6]. As a result, high-quality and adequate sleep duration serves as a natural
                               “regeneration window”, supporting performance growth, health protection, oxidative stress
                               reduction, and improved training adaptation [7].
                                     Frequent and prolonged travelling—often involving transitioning across time zones—
                               is inherent in the lifestyle of professional athletes and presents negative consequences,
                               including disruptions to the circadian rhythm, resulting in both reduced sleep quantity
                               and quality. Sleep disturbances may also manifest in less conventional ways, includ-
                               ing gastrointestinal dysfunction, impaired cognitive and executive functioning, memory
                               deficits, and emotional dysregulation. Collectively, these factors compromise recovery and
                               athletic performance.
                                     We provide a comprehensive overview of the role of sleep in sport, with particular
                               emphasis on its regenerative functions and underlying physiological, molecular, and epige-
                               netic mechanisms. Selected sleep disorders and their assessment methods are discussed,
 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                        3 of 43



                               aiming to present sleep not only as a passive state of rest but as a dynamic and essential
                               contributor to athletic performance, overall health, and injury prevention.

                               2. Methodology
                                    A narrative review was conducted using the PubMed/Medline and Cochrane
                               databases. The following English terms and their combinations were used: athletes,
                               sleep, sleep deprivation, sleep loss, sleep disorders, insomnia, exercise, sport, perfor-
                               mance, nap, physiology, pathophysiology, anxiety, stress, treatment, pharmacological, and
                               non-pharmacological.
                                    The search process was conducted stepwise. Initially, broad queries were applied,
                               such as “athletes AND sleep” (7728 results, including 3945 articles published in the last
                               five years), followed by more specific combinations targeting physiological and thera-
                               peutic aspects and focusing on studies published in the last five years. For example:
                               “athletes AND sleep AND physiology” (1259 results), “athletes AND sleep AND sleep
                               deprivation” (190 results), and “athletes AND sleep AND stress” (694 results). Additional
                               queries addressed treatment approaches, including pharmacological (157 results) and
                               non-pharmacological (36 results).
                                    Approximately 7700 publications were identified. After screening the titles and ab-
                               stracts, 178 articles were selected for evaluation. Each manuscript was then critically
                               assessed and classified into two main groups: review articles and experimental studies.
                               Subsequently, reference lists of the most relevant works were also analysed, leading to the
                               inclusion of additional papers.
                                    We excluded studies exclusively addressing psychological interventions, research
                               involving children or older adults, and papers not directly related to sleep in athletes.
                               Given the breadth of the subject, a selective choice of factors affecting sleep was made.
                               The final selection focused on literature concerning the physiology of sleep, the bidirec-
                               tional relationship between sleep and physical activity, the influence of diet and stress,
                               sleep disorders, pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments, as well as sleep
                               assessment tools.
                                    We present a simple Flow Diagram (Scheme 1) illustrating the process of literature
                               identification, screening, and inclusion.




                               Scheme 1. FLOW DIAGRAM illustrating the process of literature identification, screening
                               and inclusion.

                               3. The Physiology of Sleep
                                    Sleep constitutes a fundamental psychophysiological process indispensable for pre-
                               serving physiological capacity, health, and overall well-being, especially within athletic
                               populations. Sleep and athletic performance remain in a close, bidirectional relationship.
                               On the one hand, adequate sleep duration and quality form the foundation of recovery,
                               supporting muscle repair, hormonal regulation, and cognitive processes that underlie
 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                               4 of 43



                               decision-making and motor coordination [1–4]. Even short-term sleep deprivation leads to
                               reduced strength, power, and endurance, impaired reaction time, as well as disturbances
                               in cognitive functions—all factors that determine athletic outcomes. Chronic sleep de-
                               ficiency exacerbates catabolic processes through elevated cortisol levels and decreased
                               testosterone and growth hormone concentrations, thereby limiting protein synthesis and
                               muscle recovery capacity [4].
                                    On the other hand, physical activity itself and high training intensity influence sleep.
                               Moderate exercise can improve sleep depth and facilitate recovery, whereas excessive
                               training loads, pre-competition stress, or frequent travel across time zones may lead to
                               circadian rhythm disruptions, difficulties falling asleep, and sleep fragmentation [1–4]. In
                               young athletes, insufficient sleep increases the risk of musculoskeletal injuries, while in
                               professional athletes, it reduces training efficiency and prolongs the time required to restore
                               peak performance [3,4].
                                    The literature emphasises that extending sleep duration (“sleep extension”) improves
                               technical precision, reaction time, shooting accuracy, and aerobic performance, while short
                               naps can partly compensate for nocturnal sleep deficits and support recovery [2–4]. Conse-
                               quently, sleep is considered a key “recovery window” for athletes, with its insufficiency
                               counteracting the benefits of even the most carefully designed training program [3,4].
                                    Sleep consists of two major phases: rapid eye movement (REM) and non-rapid eye
                               movement (NREM) sleep. NREM is further divided into three distinct stages—N1, N2,
                               and N3—each characterised by specific brainwave patterns, eye movements, and levels
                               of muscle tone (Figure 1). During sleep, a healthy athlete can cycle through the sleep
                               stages approximately 4 to 6 times, with each full cycle lasting approximately 90 min. Many
                               factors influence the quality and structure of sleep, including age, mood disorders such as
                               depression, traumatic brain injuries, medications, sporting activity and circadian rhythm
                               disturbances. Detailed physiological processes involved in these changes are described
                               under the concept of “pathophysiology” [8].
                                    Human sleep is characterised by distinctive neural oscillations observable through an
                               electroencephalogram (EEG), which demonstrates the various functional stages of sleep.
                               During Stage N1, the transition from wakefulness is marked by the reduction in alpha
                               activity and the emergence of theta waves (4–7 Hz), often accompanied by vertex sharp
                               transients and slow eye movements. These low-frequency rhythms signal the brain to
                               move away from external awareness while drifting towards deeper rest [9].

 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                         5 of 43



                                     Within Stage N2, two hallmark waveforms appear: sleep spindles and K-complexes.
                               Sleep spindles consist of rhythmic bursts at 12–14 Hz lasting about 0.5–1.5 s, generated by
                               thalamocortical circuits. They act as sensory gatekeepers and play a key role in memory
                               consolidation, evidenced by increased spindle density correlating with better recall. K-
                               complexes are large, biphasic waves exceeding 100 µV, serving to protect sleep from
                               disruptions and aiding synaptic homeostasis. These too are linked to memory processes.
                               There is strong evidence confirming a correlation between the duration of stage 2 sleep
                               and the consolidation of motor memory. For athletes, sufficient time spent in stage 2 sleep
                               is crucial for the long-term retention of techniques and motor patterns, which directly
                               translates into subsequent performance [11].
                                     Stage N3, or slow-wave sleep, is defined by delta waves (0.5–4 Hz, >75 µV), which
                               reflect synchronised cortical activity facilitating physical and immune system restoration.
                               Importantly, sharp-wave ripples, the high-frequency oscillations originating in the hip-
                               pocampus, are tightly coupled with delta waves. These ripples mark moments when
                               memories are replayed and transferred from the hippocampus to the cortex for long-term
                               storage [12]. The deep sleep phase (N3) is particularly important, as this is when the
                               mechanisms enabling muscle recovery and protein synthesis are amplified. Studies have
                               demonstrated that insufficient slow-wave sleep disrupts growth hormone (GH) secretion
                               and alters cortisol levels, thereby impairing post-exercise muscle recovery. Moreover, re-
                               duced slow-wave activity promotes inflammatory processes, as sleep restriction elevates
                               pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, CRP), which hinder muscle tissue repair and delay the
                               restoration of optimal performance [4].
                                     During REM sleep, the EEG exhibits mixed, low-amplitude theta (4–8 Hz) and
                               beta/gamma (>30 Hz) activity together with REMs and muscle atonia. REM is further
                               characterised by sawtooth waves, ponto-geniculo-occipital (PGO) waves, and synchronised
                               theta–gamma oscillations. PGO waves, originating in the pons and propagating through
                               the lateral geniculate nucleus to the visual cortex, align closely with hippocampal theta,
                               supporting emotional memory processing and vivid dreaming. The coupling of theta phase
                               and gamma amplitude—especially in the hippocampus—is linked to enhanced memory
                               consolidation during REM [13] (Figure 2). In athletes, REM sleep facilitates the generation
                               of new strategies and enhances the assimilation of information by strengthening memory
                               traces associated with training.
                                     Sleep architecture provides essential conditions for hormonal regulation, anabolic
                               activity, and neurological processes. Although sleep may appear disadvantageous, because
                               it increases vulnerability to predators, limits food intake, and restricts opportunities for
                               reproduction, it persists throughout the animal kingdom. This persistence is likely ex-
                               plained by its crucial role in brain and behavioural development, as well as in memory
                               reorganisation [4]. Three main hypotheses have been proposed to explain the role of sleep
                               in the brain development of mammalian neonates. The Ontogenetic Hypothesis suggests
                               that the amount of sleep or phasic sleep activity is closely related to brain development
                               and maturation. According to the study by Frank, pharmacological deprivation of REM
                               sleep can cause abnormal brain development or behaviour [14]. The studies performed on
                               rodents have shown that it can cause changes in cholinergic and monoaminergic systems,
                               neurotransmission, and the survival of neurons [15].

                               Figure 2. Electroencephalogram (EEG) patterns during sleep stages. Created in BioRender. Kacz-
                               marek, F. (2025) https://BioRender.com/hxph7vv, (accessed on 20 October 2025).

                                     A second theory, the Consolidation Hypothesis, proposes that sleep provides a critical
                               window for consolidating experience. This process occurs primarily during developmental
                               periods of heightened, experience-dependent brain plasticity. The third explanation, the
                               Synaptic Homeostasis Hypothesis (SHY), states that sleep enables the reduction in the num-
                               ber of synapses, selectively weakening less important connections while preserving those
                               essential for transmitting critical information. This process makes room for the formation
                               of new synapses [14]. Tononi et al., in their study, describe sleep as “the price the brain
                               pays for its neuroplasticity”. Scientists agree with SHY and emphasise the role of normal
                               sleep architecture in synaptic and cellular homeostasis, which must align with the plastic
                               changes present during normal wakefulness. The balance of synaptic downscaling, learn-
                               ing processes, and synaptogenesis is necessary to prevent saturation of synaptic networks
                               and maintain neuroplasticity [16]. The study by Colavito et al. indicates that sleep depri-
                               vation, when performed correctly, results in memory dysfunction in rodents. Although
                               the study reports that sleep deprivation significantly impairs hippocampus-dependent
                               spatial memory consolidation and contextual fear memory, the cued fear memory appears
                               to remain unaffected by the loss of sleep, which shows that the effect of altered sleeping
                               affects various types of memory differently [17]. At the synaptic level, although the total
                               strength of connections underlying specific memories remains unknown, molecular, elec-
                               trophysiological, and structural markers indicate a reduction in synaptic strength in the
                               cerebral cortex and hippocampus. These findings are consistent with SHY, which proposes
                               that synaptic downscaling during sleep is balanced by the selective strengthening of con-
                               nections that support learning and memory reorganisation [18]. The duration and quality
                               of sleep influence not only the neurological processes, but also the activity of the endocrine
                               system. This is because concentrations of specific hormones, such as GH and cortisol,
 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                            7 of 43



                               exhibit sleep-related variability, suggesting the close bidirectional connection between sleep
                               and endocrine function. The study by Sassin et al. discovered that significant release of
                               GH occurs during slow-wave sleep during stages 3 and 4 [19]. Additionally, the cortisol
                               level rapidly grows about 30 min after awakening. This phenomenon is known as a cortisol
                               awakening response. Wright et al. studied the relationship between sleep deprivation,
                               circadian misalignment, and cortisol levels among other factors. In their study, they showed
                               that acute sleep deprivation increased cortisol levels during the evening and early morning
                               hours. On the other hand, chronic circadian misalignment decreased cortisol levels over
                               the 24-h day [20]. Adequate sleep duration is necessary to maintain proper hunger and
                               satiety. Spielberg et al. claimed that sleep restriction changed levels of appetite-related
                               hormones. In their study, two consecutive nights of restricted sleep (four hours in bed) in
                               young, healthy men resulted in a 24% increase in ghrelin (a hunger hormone) and an 18%
                               decrease in leptin (a hunger-suppressing hormone). Moreover, participants demonstrated
                               a stronger preference for calorie-dense foods rich in carbohydrates [21].

                               3.1. Neurochemical Mechanisms of Sleep and Wakefulness
                                     The inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) plays a crucial
                               role in initiating sleep by binding to GABA-A receptors in the brain [22]. Sleep-promoting
                               neurons in the anterior hypothalamus release GABA, which suppresses wake-promoting
                               regions in the hypothalamus and brainstem. GABA plays a central role in promoting
                               slow-wave sleep, thereby supporting athletes’ physical recovery, hormonal balance, and
                               muscle repair following intensive exercise. Adenosine also facilitates sleep by inhibiting
                               orexinergic neurons in the hypothalamus while activating neurons in the preoptic area.
                               Through its progressive accumulation during wakefulness, it promotes sleep pressure and
                               facilitates recovery processes, making it a critical factor in athletes’ restoration of physical
                               performance and prevention of overtraining [23,24].
                                     Conversely, neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine (ACh), dopamine, norepinephrine,
                               serotonin, histamine, and orexin peptides work together to maintain wakefulness. In ath-
                               letes, these mechanisms are particularly important, as effective activation of the arousal
                               system influences vigilance, reaction time, motor coordination, and physical performance.
                               Regular physical training can modulate the functioning of these neurochemical pathways,
                               leading to increased dopaminergic and noradrenergic activity and optimized orexin release,
                               which supports better regulation of circadian rhythms, energy levels, and adaptive capacity
                               to physical exertion. Acetylcholine release is highest during both wakefulness and REM
                               sleep, but significantly lower during NREM [23]. Serotonin is produced by neurons in the
                               raphe nuclei, norepinephrine by the locus coeruleus, and histamine by the tuberomam-
                               millary nucleus of the posterior hypothalamus. Orexin, synthesised in the hypothalamus,
                               communicates with key arousal centres to sustain alertness [24].
                                     Sleep is intertwined with the circadian rhythms that are linked to the daily rhythms
                               of temperature and light. Throughout evolution, this linkage became more nuanced, but
                               the basic rest-activity cycles still play a role in the life of organisms. Human sleep is a
                               result of a series of molecules that are released locally, and when their effects are summed,
                               they change the activity of the entire system [25]. These molecules play a significant role
                               in keeping us asleep and awake. The level of dopamine, an important neurotransmitter
                               that affects reward-motivated behaviour, increases during the night and is controlled by
                               the circadian rhythms. The decrease in serotonin (5-HT), which regulates emotions and
                               mental well-being, can disrupt the rest-activity cycle. Glutamate, on the other hand, sends
                               information about the presence of light from the retino-hypothalamic tract (RHT) to the
                               hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), which induces changes in sleep phases
                               and increases during the day. Norepinephrine, which modulates attention, arousal, and
 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                                    8 of 43



                                       cognition, increases during the night and stimulates the production of melatonin. Melatonin
                                       is a hormone produced by the pineal gland that regulates sleep onset and latency [26].
                                       All of those substances and many more play a significant role in the process of sleeping.
                                       In athletes, a balanced regulation of these neurotransmitters and hormones is crucial for
                                       efficient recovery, maintenance of physical performance, and adaptation to training loads.
                                       Adenosine triphosphate (ATP), adenosine, nitric oxide (NO), prostaglandins, interleukin-1β
                                       (IL-1β), tumour necrosis factor α (TNF-α), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and
                                       nerve growth factor (NGF) all regulate sleep when released [25].
                                             Sleep requirements and architecture vary significantly depending on age [Table 1].
                                       During early life, sleep is longer and less consolidated, while in adulthood, it becomes
                                       shorter and more fragmented. Table 1 summarises these developmental changes in sleep
                                       patterns, circadian rhythms, and predominant sleep stages. Younger athletes may require
                                       longer sleep to support neurodevelopment, motor learning, and adaptation to increasing
                                       training loads. In adult athletes, shorter and more fragmented sleep can compromise
                                       recovery, cognitive function, and performance if not adequately managed [23–25].
