405	                                       3.2. Physiological and Molecular Benefits of Sleep
406	                                            Adequate sleep has shown various advantages, including a regenerative effect on
407	                                       tissues and improvement in physical performance. Chen et al. investigated the association
408	                                       of sleep-disordered breathing and healing of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs). The apnoea-
409	                                       hypoapnoea index (AHI) did not show a significant correlation with wound healing;
410	                                       however, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, and wakefulness after sleep onset (WASO)
411	                                       were associated with healing. Sleep fragmentation and hypoxemia predicted poor wound
412	                                       healing, high risk of ulcer recurrence, and even death in patients with DFUs [31]. Luo et al.
413	                                       suggested that circadian rhythms are intricately linked to bone reconstruction. The cycles
414	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                          9 of 43
415	
416	
417	
418	                               of rest-activity affect bone energy metabolism by controlling the expression of the genes
419	                               corresponding to dentin matrix protein 1 (Dmp1), osteopontin (Spp1), bone sialoprotein
420	                               (Bsp), and osteocalcin (Bglap2), which participate in mineral deposition in the bones [32].
421	                               Elkhenany et al. observed how temperature changes, pH, carbon dioxide (CO2) level, NO,
422	                               and hormone production affect stem cells during sleep. Specific levels of these parameters
423	                               can stimulate growth, proliferation, differentiation, and self-renewal. Lung repair and
424	                               regeneration are also affected by circadian rhythms [33].
425	                                     Recently, the significance of sleep and its vital contribution to athletic performance,
426	                               cognitive function, overall health, and psychological well-being have received growing
427	                               recognition. Research consistently demonstrates that sleep restriction negatively affects
428	                               physical performance in both submaximal and maximal efforts. Following sleep depri-
429	                               vation, physiological strain increases, as evidenced by elevated heart rate, ventilation,
430	                               respiratory frequency, and lactate accumulation, which collectively lead to earlier onset of
431	                               fatigue and reductions in VO2 max. Sleep restriction also impairs anaerobic power, move-
432	                               ment accuracy, muscle strength, and glycogen resynthesis, thereby limiting endurance
433	                               and recovery capacity. Prolonged sleep deprivation further disrupts autonomic nervous
434	                               system balance, potentially promoting overtraining-like states, whereas its effects on basic
435	                               cardiorespiratory function appear less consistent and are likely dependent on the mode,
436	                               intensity, and duration of exercise [34]. Acute sleep deprivation significantly impairs ath-
437	                               letes’ sporting performance, with medium to large effect sizes depending on the type of
438	                               performance and timing of assessment. The mechanisms underlying this decline include
439	                               depletion of energy reserves, particularly muscle and liver glycogen, which limits the
440	                               body’s ability to sustain and resynthesize energy during exercise. Cognitive impairments,
441	                               such as reduced working memory, attention, and executive function, further compromise
442	                               skill execution and decision-making. Additionally, sleep deprivation disrupts sleep ar-
443	                               chitecture and increases inflammatory markers, negatively affecting muscle recovery and
444	                               function. Performance decrements are most pronounced in high-intensity intermittent
445	                               exercise, skill-based tasks, explosive power, and speed, with afternoon testing showing
446	                               greater impairments than morning sessions. These effects are mediated by altered percep-
447	                               tion of fatigue, circadian rhythm disturbances, and sleep homeostasis, including adenosine
448	                               accumulation, which collectively reduce neuromuscular efficiency, hormonal regulation,
449	                               and overall physical capacity [35].
450	                                     Adequate sleep and properly synchronised circadian rhythms enhance tissue repair,
451	                               bone remodelling, and cellular regeneration in athletes by regulating the expression of
452	                               genes involved in these regenerative processes, supporting recovery, adaptation to train-
453	                               ing, and peak performance. Conversely, sleep fragmentation, reduced sleep efficiency, or
454	                               disrupted circadian cycles can impair these gene-mediated mechanisms, compromising
455	                               recovery, diminishing performance, and increasing injury risk. Although all the above
456	                               mechanisms of circadian rhythms and sleep can affect tissue regeneration and, conse-
457	                               quently, the performance of athletes, it is essential to further research this area to draw
458	                               firm correlations.
459	
460	                               Molecular Consequences of Sleep Loss: Apoptosis and Circadian Disruption
461	                                    The expression of genes associated with cell survival and death can be influenced by
462	                               behavioural stressors like sleep deprivation and strenuous activity. In a study involving
463	                               20 healthy male participants, Norouzi Kamareh and colleagues found that 24-h sleep
464	                               deprivation combined with anaerobic sprint testing significantly elevated pro-apoptotic
465	                               markers: Bcl-2 associated X protein (BAX) and cell cycle and apoptosis regulator 2 (CCAR2),
466	                               while simultaneously reducing anti-apoptotic: B-cell lymphoma protein 2 (BCL2) and the
467	                               circadian regulator brain and muscle ARNT-like protein 1 (BMAL1) in peripheral blood
468	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                         10 of 43
469	
470	
471	
472	                               mononuclear cells (PBMCs) (p < 0.05) [36]. This suggests that in athletes, particularly under
473	                               conditions of sleep deprivation and high-intensity training, cellular stress and apoptotic
474	                               signalling may be markedly increased, potentially impacting recovery and adaptation. BAX
475	                               promotes mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation, an essential step in initiating
476	                               apoptosis. CCAR2, meanwhile, intensifies p53-dependent apoptotic signalling, partly
477	                               by downregulating BMAL1 through sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) inhibition [37]. Conversely, BCL2
478	                               stabilises mitochondrial membranes and inhibits apoptosis, while BMAL1 is known to
479	                               support cellular rhythmicity and survival pathways [38].
480	                                     L-arginine supplementation (1000 mg/day over eight weeks) appeared to reverse
481	                               many of these effects. Treated individuals showed increased expression of BCL2 and
482	                               BMAL1 and reduced levels of BAX and CCAR2 when compared to the effect of placebo
483	                               controls [36]. This indicates that in athletic populations, L-arginine supplementation may
484	                               help mitigate the pro-apoptotic effects associated with sleep deprivation and strenuous
485	                               exercise, potentially supporting cellular recovery and adaptation. These observations are
486	                               consistent with the capacity of L-arginine to modulate NO pathways and oxidative stress,
487	                               both of which are connected to cell survival signalling [39].
488	                                     Short-term sleep deprivation can lead to measurable cardiovascular strain. Yang
489	                               et al. reported that subjects who remained awake for 24 h exhibited elevated resting blood
490	                               pressure and an amplified pressor response to submaximal isometric exercise [40]. This was
491	                               partly attributed to impaired baroreflex sensitivity and heightened sympathetic nervous
492	                               system activation, as previously shown by Ogawa et al. [41].
493	                                     Further evidence from Hori et al. indicated that a 2-h sleep during a deprivation
494	                               period failed to mitigate these hemodynamic changes, pointing to the inadequacy of brief
495	                               sleep recovery in resetting cardiovascular homeostasis [42]. Kato and Mullington also
496	                               emphasised the role of sympathetic overdrive and inflammatory pathways in sleep loss–
497	                               induced circulatory dysregulation [43,44]. For athletes, such responses may not only impair
498	                               performance but may raise long-term risks for cardiovascular disease, particularly with
499	                               repeated bouts of sleep deprivation.
500	                                     Beyond systemic physiology, sleep loss exerts significant effects on multiple levels of
501	                               human function, which is particularly relevant for athletes and individuals involved in high-
502	                               intensity or physically demanding training. From a neurophysiological perspective, sleep
503	                               loss can impair cognitive and motor function, which are critical for athletic performance.
504	                               Controlled studies using positron emission tomography (PET) imaging have shown that
505	                               even a single night of sleep deprivation leads to increased accumulation of β-amyloid in
506	                               brain regions such as the hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and thalamus, which in
507	                               athletes may contribute to slower reaction times, impaired decision-making, and reduced
508	                               coordination during training or competition [45,46]. Fragmented or insufficient sleep
509	                               also disrupts connectivity between key neural regions, such as the prefrontal cortex and
510	                               amygdala, affecting mood, attention, and stress regulation—factors directly impacting
511	                               performance and recovery [47,48]. These neurobiological effects, observed even after
512	                               short-term sleep loss, underscore the importance of uninterrupted, restorative sleep for
513	                               maintaining optimal cognitive and motor function in physically active populations [49,50].
514	                                     Acute sleep deprivation has been shown to shift gene expression toward pro-apoptotic
515	                               pathways, increasing levels of BAX and CCAR2, while simultaneously reducing anti-
516	                               apoptotic BCL2 and circadian regulator BMAL1 in peripheral blood mononuclear cells,
517	                               potentially compromising cellular survival and rhythmicity [36]. Interventions such as L-
518	                               arginine supplementation (1000 mg/day over eight weeks) have been shown to counteract
519	                               some of the molecular stress effects induced by sleep deprivation, increasing BCL2 and
520	                               BMAL1 expression and reducing BAX and CCAR2 levels compared to placebo, potentially
521	                               supporting both cellular and neural resilience [36,39] (Figure 3).
522	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                            11 of 43
523	
524	
525	
526	
527	                               Figure 3. Gene expression changes linking sleep deprivation and anaerobic exercise to apopto-
528	                               sis. Created in BioRender. Kaczmarek, F. (2025) https://BioRender.com/igapu4d, (accessed on
529	                               20 October 2025).
530	
531	                                    From a cardiovascular standpoint, controlled 24-h sleep deprivation combined with
532	                               submaximal isometric exercise elevates resting arterial blood pressure and exaggerates
533	                               the pressor response to physical exertion. Even short recovery naps (e.g., 2 h) were insuf-
534	                               ficient to normalise these exaggerated hemodynamic responses, emphasising the critical
535	                               importance of continuous restorative sleep for cardiovascular stability and athletic perfor-
536	                               mance [42].
537	                                    Altogether, these findings highlight that acute sleep deprivation, especially when
538	                               combined with intense physical activity, can compromise cellular, cardiovascular, and
539	                               neurophysiological systems in athletic populations. Increased β-amyloid accumulation in
540	                               athletes due to insufficient sleep may further impair cognitive performance and recovery,
541	                               making sufficient, high-quality sleep essential for maintaining peak performance, proper
542	                               decision-making, and overall physiological resilience.
543	
544	                               4. Methods and Tools for Assessing Sleep Quality and Duration
545	                                    Research on sleep in athletes leverages advances in technologies, tools, and ques-
546	                               tionnaires designed to measure, monitor, and evaluate sleep in this population. Different
547	                               methods of sleep assessment vary in terms of validity and reliability, and the choice of
548	                               method depends largely on the specific purpose of monitoring. Objective measures, such
549	                               as polysomnography (PSG) and actigraphy, provide quantitative data on sleep architecture,
550	                               duration, efficiency, and fragmentation. PSG is considered the gold standard for evaluating
551	                               detailed sleep stages but is resource-intensive and often limited to laboratory settings, while
552	                               actigraphy allows for longitudinal, field-based monitoring, albeit with lower specificity for
553	                               sleep stages. Subjective tools, including questionnaires like the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality
554	                               Index (PSQI) or the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire (ASSQ), capture perceived sleep
555	                               quality and disturbances but may be influenced by individual bias or recall inaccuracies.
556	                               Sleep trackers, including wearable and nearable devices, represent some of the most rapidly
557	                               evolving tools in this field. Most studies focus on the effects of sleep restriction or depriva-
558	                               tion, as well as the cumulative impact of sleep deficit, on various physiological functions
559	                               and athletic performance. The use of heterogeneous assessment methods frequently results
560	                               in divergent findings, complicating direct comparisons and synthesis. Consequently, in-
561	                               terpreting the influence of dietary or lifestyle interventions on sleep in athletes requires
562	                               careful consideration of the measurement approach, and conclusions are often contingent
563	                               on whether objective or subjective metrics were employed [51,52].
564	                                    Proper sleep is often defined using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), devel-
565	                               oped by Buysse et al. (1989) [53] to assess sleep quality. It contains 19 questions covering
566	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                          12 of 43
567	
568	
569	
570	                               quality, duration, latency, efficiency, disturbances, medication use, and daytime dysfunc-
571	                               tion. A PSQI score > 5 indicates poor sleep, while scores ≤ 5 indicate good sleep [53].
572	                               After 35 years of use, updates have been proposed, including the shorter PSQI-2 (De
573	                               Menezes-Júnior et al., 2025) based on sleep duration and subjective quality (0–6 points,
574	                               higher = worse sleep) [51].
575	                                    Polysomnography (PSG) records sleep using a camera and multiple sensors, analysed
576	                               by technicians. Reports include the AHI, with scores < 5/hour considered normal; higher
577	                               values may suggest sleep apnoea [52]. Although PSG produces an accurate assessment
578	                               of nocturnal sleep, it is invasive and less accessible. Actigraphy (ACG), using wearable
579	                               devices to track movement and light over multiple days at home, is non-invasive but less
580	                               precise as it relies solely on movement [54]; Zeiter et al. found increased discrepancies with
581	                               PSG when wake time during a sleep episode is longer [55].
582	                                    PSQI and ACG studies are most commonly used on athletes—both are non-invasive
583	                               and easy to use in the home environment. Other tools include sleep diaries (e.g., Consensus
584	                               Sleep Diary [56]), chronotype scales (MEQ, MCTQ), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) [57],
585	                               Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS) [58], and Athlete Sleep Behaviour Questionnaire (ASBQ) [59].
586	                               All require patient cooperation to ensure reliable results.
587	
588	                               5. Sleep and Performance in Athletes: Selected External Factors
589	                                     Sleep quality in athletes can be disrupted by various environmental factors—such
590	                               as diet, transmeridian travel, and ambient conditions—that can significantly affect their
591	                               recovery and performance.
592	                                     Travelling across at least four time zones leads to a desynchronisation of the circadian
593	                               rhythm, resulting in jet lag symptoms such as sleep disturbances, difficulty concentrating,
594	                               irritability, mild depression, fatigue, and gastrointestinal problems. In athletes, this may
595	                               lead to reduced physical and mental performance as well as an increased risk of injury [60].
596	                               The direction of travel plays a critical role in the adaptation process. East–west travel
597	                               is generally associated with more adverse effects compared to north–south travel. A
598	                               study analysing 20 years of data from Major League Baseball demonstrated that eastward
599	                               travel exerted a significantly greater negative impact on winning percentages compared to
600	                               westward travel, with this effect reaching statistical significance only for home teams, which
601	                               experienced an approximate 3.5% decrease in wins (p < 0.05) [61]. For most individuals,
602	                               eastward travel poses greater adaptation challenges than westward travel, though this is
603	                               not universally the case. Eastward transitions require an advancement of the circadian
604	                               rhythm, a process that is inherently more difficult, while westward travel induces a phase
605	                               delay. In the latter case, competition times may coincide with the biological night of the
606	                               athlete, significantly impairing physical and cognitive performance. While in the short
607	                               term, jet lag may reduce the likelihood of optimal performance or victory, chronic travel
608	                               across time zones, particularly in the east–west direction, acts as a potent physiological
609	                               and psychological stressor. This is associated with increased risk of injury, cognitive
610	                               impairments, and mood disturbances [61] (Figure 4).
611	                                     The impact of circadian misalignment and associated sleep deficits on athletic perfor-
612	                               mance and health varies across sports disciplines. For example, aerobic training requires
613	                               greater energy expenditure than anaerobic training, and as such, endurance athletes gen-
614	                               erally exhibit a higher sleep need [62]. These observations underscore the necessity for
615	                               a discipline-specific and individualised approach to training schedules and competition
616	                               planning. Although circadian disruption affects athletic performance, its influence is often
617	                               difficult to predict due to the interplay of multiple factors such as travel logistics, light
618	                               exposure, and event timing.
619	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                            13 of 43
620	
621	
622	
623	
624	                               Figure 4. Effects of travel direction on circadian rhythm and athletic performance. Created in
625	                               BioRender. Kaczmarek, F. (2025) https://BioRender.com/5mzouop, (accessed on 20 October 2025).
626	
627	                                    To mitigate these adverse effects, the following recommendations have been proposed
628	                               to enable circadian adaptation:
629	                               (1)   Pre-adaptation—gradually shift sleep timing by 30–60 min in the days preceding
630	                                     travel, combined with appropriate light exposure (morning light for eastward travel,
631	                                     evening light for westward travel),
632	                               (2)   Post-arrival adaptation—adjust sleep, light exposure, meals, and training schedules
633	                                     to the local time zone, avoiding bright light at inappropriate times,
634	                               (3)   Recovery—allow a minimum of 24 h rest following travel; naps lasting 20–90 min can
635	                                     support physical and cognitive performance,
636	                               (4)   Sleep hygiene—limit caffeine intake and screen exposure in the evening, utilise eye
637	                                     masks and earplugs, and avoid intensive activities immediately after waking,
638	                               (5)   Technological support and education—use apps for planning light exposure and
639	                                     caffeine use; provide education on sleep and circadian rhythms for athletes and
640	                                     support staff [63] (Figure 5).
641	                                    Diet plays a significant role in the sleep quality of athletes. The most cited dietary fac-
642	                               tors associated with improved sleep in general populations include meal timing, macronu-
643	                               trient composition, and supplementation [64]. The timing and composition of meals act
644	                               as key zeitgebers (external time cues, e.g., light or meal timing) for peripheral molecular
645	                               oscillators, particularly within hepatic and gastrointestinal tissues. Disruptions in feeding
646	                               rhythms can induce desynchronization between peripheral clocks and the central pace-
647	                               maker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, resulting in impaired glucose and lipid homeostasis,
648	                               altered hormonal secretion, and heightened systemic inflammation. In athletes, such circa-

650	                               metabolism during exercise, modulate endocrine responses (e.g., cortisol, testosterone,

                                       3.2. Physiological and Molecular Benefits of Sleep
                                            Adequate sleep has shown various advantages, including a regenerative effect on
                                       tissues and improvement in physical performance. Chen et al. investigated the association
                                       of sleep-disordered breathing and healing of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs). The apnoea-
                                       hypoapnoea index (AHI) did not show a significant correlation with wound healing;
                                       however, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, and wakefulness after sleep onset (WASO)
                                       were associated with healing. Sleep fragmentation and hypoxemia predicted poor wound
                                       healing, high risk of ulcer recurrence, and even death in patients with DFUs [31]. Luo et al.
                                       suggested that circadian rhythms are intricately linked to bone reconstruction. The cycles
 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                          9 of 43



                               of rest-activity affect bone energy metabolism by controlling the expression of the genes
                               corresponding to dentin matrix protein 1 (Dmp1), osteopontin (Spp1), bone sialoprotein
                               (Bsp), and osteocalcin (Bglap2), which participate in mineral deposition in the bones [32].
                               Elkhenany et al. observed how temperature changes, pH, carbon dioxide (CO2) level, NO,
                               and hormone production affect stem cells during sleep. Specific levels of these parameters
                               can stimulate growth, proliferation, differentiation, and self-renewal. Lung repair and
                               regeneration are also affected by circadian rhythms [33].
                                     Recently, the significance of sleep and its vital contribution to athletic performance,
                               cognitive function, overall health, and psychological well-being have received growing
                               recognition. Research consistently demonstrates that sleep restriction negatively affects
                               physical performance in both submaximal and maximal efforts. Following sleep depri-
                               vation, physiological strain increases, as evidenced by elevated heart rate, ventilation,
                               respiratory frequency, and lactate accumulation, which collectively lead to earlier onset of
                               fatigue and reductions in VO2 max. Sleep restriction also impairs anaerobic power, move-
                               ment accuracy, muscle strength, and glycogen resynthesis, thereby limiting endurance
                               and recovery capacity. Prolonged sleep deprivation further disrupts autonomic nervous
                               system balance, potentially promoting overtraining-like states, whereas its effects on basic
                               cardiorespiratory function appear less consistent and are likely dependent on the mode,
                               intensity, and duration of exercise [34]. Acute sleep deprivation significantly impairs ath-
                               letes’ sporting performance, with medium to large effect sizes depending on the type of
                               performance and timing of assessment. The mechanisms underlying this decline include
                               depletion of energy reserves, particularly muscle and liver glycogen, which limits the
                               body’s ability to sustain and resynthesize energy during exercise. Cognitive impairments,
                               such as reduced working memory, attention, and executive function, further compromise
                               skill execution and decision-making. Additionally, sleep deprivation disrupts sleep ar-
                               chitecture and increases inflammatory markers, negatively affecting muscle recovery and
                               function. Performance decrements are most pronounced in high-intensity intermittent
                               exercise, skill-based tasks, explosive power, and speed, with afternoon testing showing
                               greater impairments than morning sessions. These effects are mediated by altered percep-
                               tion of fatigue, circadian rhythm disturbances, and sleep homeostasis, including adenosine
                               accumulation, which collectively reduce neuromuscular efficiency, hormonal regulation,
                               and overall physical capacity [35].
                                     Adequate sleep and properly synchronised circadian rhythms enhance tissue repair,
                               bone remodelling, and cellular regeneration in athletes by regulating the expression of
                               genes involved in these regenerative processes, supporting recovery, adaptation to train-
                               ing, and peak performance. Conversely, sleep fragmentation, reduced sleep efficiency, or
                               disrupted circadian cycles can impair these gene-mediated mechanisms, compromising
                               recovery, diminishing performance, and increasing injury risk. Although all the above
                               mechanisms of circadian rhythms and sleep can affect tissue regeneration and, conse-
                               quently, the performance of athletes, it is essential to further research this area to draw
                               firm correlations.

                               Molecular Consequences of Sleep Loss: Apoptosis and Circadian Disruption
                                    The expression of genes associated with cell survival and death can be influenced by
                               behavioural stressors like sleep deprivation and strenuous activity. In a study involving
                               20 healthy male participants, Norouzi Kamareh and colleagues found that 24-h sleep
                               deprivation combined with anaerobic sprint testing significantly elevated pro-apoptotic
                               markers: Bcl-2 associated X protein (BAX) and cell cycle and apoptosis regulator 2 (CCAR2),
                               while simultaneously reducing anti-apoptotic: B-cell lymphoma protein 2 (BCL2) and the
                               circadian regulator brain and muscle ARNT-like protein 1 (BMAL1) in peripheral blood
 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                         10 of 43



                               mononuclear cells (PBMCs) (p < 0.05) [36]. This suggests that in athletes, particularly under
                               conditions of sleep deprivation and high-intensity training, cellular stress and apoptotic
                               signalling may be markedly increased, potentially impacting recovery and adaptation. BAX
                               promotes mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation, an essential step in initiating
                               apoptosis. CCAR2, meanwhile, intensifies p53-dependent apoptotic signalling, partly
                               by downregulating BMAL1 through sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) inhibition [37]. Conversely, BCL2
                               stabilises mitochondrial membranes and inhibits apoptosis, while BMAL1 is known to
                               support cellular rhythmicity and survival pathways [38].
                                     L-arginine supplementation (1000 mg/day over eight weeks) appeared to reverse
                               many of these effects. Treated individuals showed increased expression of BCL2 and
                               BMAL1 and reduced levels of BAX and CCAR2 when compared to the effect of placebo
                               controls [36]. This indicates that in athletic populations, L-arginine supplementation may
                               help mitigate the pro-apoptotic effects associated with sleep deprivation and strenuous
                               exercise, potentially supporting cellular recovery and adaptation. These observations are
                               consistent with the capacity of L-arginine to modulate NO pathways and oxidative stress,
                               both of which are connected to cell survival signalling [39].
                                     Short-term sleep deprivation can lead to measurable cardiovascular strain. Yang
                               et al. reported that subjects who remained awake for 24 h exhibited elevated resting blood
                               pressure and an amplified pressor response to submaximal isometric exercise [40]. This was
                               partly attributed to impaired baroreflex sensitivity and heightened sympathetic nervous
                               system activation, as previously shown by Ogawa et al. [41].
                                     Further evidence from Hori et al. indicated that a 2-h sleep during a deprivation
                               period failed to mitigate these hemodynamic changes, pointing to the inadequacy of brief
                               sleep recovery in resetting cardiovascular homeostasis [42]. Kato and Mullington also
                               emphasised the role of sympathetic overdrive and inflammatory pathways in sleep loss–
                               induced circulatory dysregulation [43,44]. For athletes, such responses may not only impair
                               performance but may raise long-term risks for cardiovascular disease, particularly with
                               repeated bouts of sleep deprivation.
                                     Beyond systemic physiology, sleep loss exerts significant effects on multiple levels of
                               human function, which is particularly relevant for athletes and individuals involved in high-
                               intensity or physically demanding training. From a neurophysiological perspective, sleep
                               loss can impair cognitive and motor function, which are critical for athletic performance.
                               Controlled studies using positron emission tomography (PET) imaging have shown that
                               even a single night of sleep deprivation leads to increased accumulation of β-amyloid in
                               brain regions such as the hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and thalamus, which in
                               athletes may contribute to slower reaction times, impaired decision-making, and reduced
                               coordination during training or competition [45,46]. Fragmented or insufficient sleep
                               also disrupts connectivity between key neural regions, such as the prefrontal cortex and
                               amygdala, affecting mood, attention, and stress regulation—factors directly impacting
                               performance and recovery [47,48]. These neurobiological effects, observed even after
                               short-term sleep loss, underscore the importance of uninterrupted, restorative sleep for
                               maintaining optimal cognitive and motor function in physically active populations [49,50].
                                     Acute sleep deprivation has been shown to shift gene expression toward pro-apoptotic
                               pathways, increasing levels of BAX and CCAR2, while simultaneously reducing anti-
                               apoptotic BCL2 and circadian regulator BMAL1 in peripheral blood mononuclear cells,
                               potentially compromising cellular survival and rhythmicity [36]. Interventions such as L-
                               arginine supplementation (1000 mg/day over eight weeks) have been shown to counteract
                               some of the molecular stress effects induced by sleep deprivation, increasing BCL2 and
                               BMAL1 expression and reducing BAX and CCAR2 levels compared to placebo, potentially
                               supporting both cellular and neural resilience [36,39] (Figure 3).

                                    From a cardiovascular standpoint, controlled 24-h sleep deprivation combined with
                               submaximal isometric exercise elevates resting arterial blood pressure and exaggerates
                               the pressor response to physical exertion. Even short recovery naps (e.g., 2 h) were insuf-
                               ficient to normalise these exaggerated hemodynamic responses, emphasising the critical
                               importance of continuous restorative sleep for cardiovascular stability and athletic perfor-
                               mance [42].
                                    Altogether, these findings highlight that acute sleep deprivation, especially when
                               combined with intense physical activity, can compromise cellular, cardiovascular, and
                               neurophysiological systems in athletic populations. Increased β-amyloid accumulation in
                               athletes due to insufficient sleep may further impair cognitive performance and recovery,
                               making sufficient, high-quality sleep essential for maintaining peak performance, proper
                               decision-making, and overall physiological resilience.

                               4. Methods and Tools for Assessing Sleep Quality and Duration
                                    Research on sleep in athletes leverages advances in technologies, tools, and ques-
                               tionnaires designed to measure, monitor, and evaluate sleep in this population. Different
                               methods of sleep assessment vary in terms of validity and reliability, and the choice of
                               method depends largely on the specific purpose of monitoring. Objective measures, such
                               as polysomnography (PSG) and actigraphy, provide quantitative data on sleep architecture,
                               duration, efficiency, and fragmentation. PSG is considered the gold standard for evaluating
                               detailed sleep stages but is resource-intensive and often limited to laboratory settings, while
                               actigraphy allows for longitudinal, field-based monitoring, albeit with lower specificity for
                               sleep stages. Subjective tools, including questionnaires like the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality
                               Index (PSQI) or the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire (ASSQ), capture perceived sleep
                               quality and disturbances but may be influenced by individual bias or recall inaccuracies.
                               Sleep trackers, including wearable and nearable devices, represent some of the most rapidly
                               evolving tools in this field. Most studies focus on the effects of sleep restriction or depriva-
                               tion, as well as the cumulative impact of sleep deficit, on various physiological functions
                               and athletic performance. The use of heterogeneous assessment methods frequently results
                               in divergent findings, complicating direct comparisons and synthesis. Consequently, in-
                               terpreting the influence of dietary or lifestyle interventions on sleep in athletes requires
                               careful consideration of the measurement approach, and conclusions are often contingent
                               on whether objective or subjective metrics were employed [51,52].
                                    Proper sleep is often defined using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), devel-
                               oped by Buysse et al. (1989) [53] to assess sleep quality. It contains 19 questions covering
 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                          12 of 43



                               quality, duration, latency, efficiency, disturbances, medication use, and daytime dysfunc-
                               tion. A PSQI score > 5 indicates poor sleep, while scores ≤ 5 indicate good sleep [53].
                               After 35 years of use, updates have been proposed, including the shorter PSQI-2 (De
                               Menezes-Júnior et al., 2025) based on sleep duration and subjective quality (0–6 points,
                               higher = worse sleep) [51].
                                    Polysomnography (PSG) records sleep using a camera and multiple sensors, analysed
                               by technicians. Reports include the AHI, with scores < 5/hour considered normal; higher
                               values may suggest sleep apnoea [52]. Although PSG produces an accurate assessment
                               of nocturnal sleep, it is invasive and less accessible. Actigraphy (ACG), using wearable
                               devices to track movement and light over multiple days at home, is non-invasive but less
                               precise as it relies solely on movement [54]; Zeiter et al. found increased discrepancies with
                               PSG when wake time during a sleep episode is longer [55].
                                    PSQI and ACG studies are most commonly used on athletes—both are non-invasive
                               and easy to use in the home environment. Other tools include sleep diaries (e.g., Consensus
                               Sleep Diary [56]), chronotype scales (MEQ, MCTQ), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) [57],
                               Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS) [58], and Athlete Sleep Behaviour Questionnaire (ASBQ) [59].
                               All require patient cooperation to ensure reliable results.

                               5. Sleep and Performance in Athletes: Selected External Factors
                                     Sleep quality in athletes can be disrupted by various environmental factors—such
                               as diet, transmeridian travel, and ambient conditions—that can significantly affect their
                               recovery and performance.
                                     Travelling across at least four time zones leads to a desynchronisation of the circadian
                               rhythm, resulting in jet lag symptoms such as sleep disturbances, difficulty concentrating,
                               irritability, mild depression, fatigue, and gastrointestinal problems. In athletes, this may
                               lead to reduced physical and mental performance as well as an increased risk of injury [60].
                               The direction of travel plays a critical role in the adaptation process. East–west travel
                               is generally associated with more adverse effects compared to north–south travel. A
                               study analysing 20 years of data from Major League Baseball demonstrated that eastward
                               travel exerted a significantly greater negative impact on winning percentages compared to
                               westward travel, with this effect reaching statistical significance only for home teams, which
                               experienced an approximate 3.5% decrease in wins (p < 0.05) [61]. For most individuals,
                               eastward travel poses greater adaptation challenges than westward travel, though this is
                               not universally the case. Eastward transitions require an advancement of the circadian
                               rhythm, a process that is inherently more difficult, while westward travel induces a phase
                               delay. In the latter case, competition times may coincide with the biological night of the
                               athlete, significantly impairing physical and cognitive performance. While in the short
                               term, jet lag may reduce the likelihood of optimal performance or victory, chronic travel
                               across time zones, particularly in the east–west direction, acts as a potent physiological
                               and psychological stressor. This is associated with increased risk of injury, cognitive
                               impairments, and mood disturbances [61] (Figure 4).
                                     The impact of circadian misalignment and associated sleep deficits on athletic perfor-
                               mance and health varies across sports disciplines. For example, aerobic training requires
                               greater energy expenditure than anaerobic training, and as such, endurance athletes gen-
                               erally exhibit a higher sleep need [62]. These observations underscore the necessity for
                               a discipline-specific and individualised approach to training schedules and competition
                               planning. Although circadian disruption affects athletic performance, its influence is often
                               difficult to predict due to the interplay of multiple factors such as travel logistics, light
                               exposure, and event timing.

                                    To mitigate these adverse effects, the following recommendations have been proposed
                               to enable circadian adaptation:
                               (1)   Pre-adaptation—gradually shift sleep timing by 30–60 min in the days preceding
                                     travel, combined with appropriate light exposure (morning light for eastward travel,
                                     evening light for westward travel),
                               (2)   Post-arrival adaptation—adjust sleep, light exposure, meals, and training schedules
                                     to the local time zone, avoiding bright light at inappropriate times,
                               (3)   Recovery—allow a minimum of 24 h rest following travel; naps lasting 20–90 min can
                                     support physical and cognitive performance,
                               (4)   Sleep hygiene—limit caffeine intake and screen exposure in the evening, utilise eye
                                     masks and earplugs, and avoid intensive activities immediately after waking,
                               (5)   Technological support and education—use apps for planning light exposure and
                                     caffeine use; provide education on sleep and circadian rhythms for athletes and
                                     support staff [63] (Figure 5).
                                    Diet plays a significant role in the sleep quality of athletes. The most cited dietary fac-
                               tors associated with improved sleep in general populations include meal timing, macronu-
                               trient composition, and supplementation [64]. The timing and composition of meals act
                               as key zeitgebers (external time cues, e.g., light or meal timing) for peripheral molecular
                               oscillators, particularly within hepatic and gastrointestinal tissues. Disruptions in feeding
                               rhythms can induce desynchronization between peripheral clocks and the central pace-
                               maker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, resulting in impaired glucose and lipid homeostasis,
                               altered hormonal secretion, and heightened systemic inflammation. In athletes, such circa-
                               dian misalignment may have significant consequences: it can negatively affect substrate
                               metabolism during exercise, modulate endocrine responses (e.g., cortisol, testosterone,
                               growth hormone), and disturb sleep architecture and recovery processes. Consequently,
                               misalignment between feeding schedules and circadian rhythms may reduce exercise ca-
                               pacity, prolong recovery time, and increase susceptibility to injury and overtraining [65].
                               Consuming tryptophan-rich foods (such as turkey, fish, eggs, yoghurt, and nuts) and com-
                               plex carbohydrates can enhance the production of melatonin—the hormone responsible
 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                                   14 of 43



                               for regulating sleep. Melatonin levels appear to be sensitive to dietary macronutrient
                               composition, with protein and carbohydrate intake indirectly affecting its biosynthesis
                               through modulation of the tryptophan to large neutral amino acid ratio. An increase in
                               this ratio may enhance the availability of tryptophan, stimulate melatonin synthesis, and
                               consequently improve sleep, which can be achieved through the consumption of carbohy-
                               drates or protein sources that are high in tryptophan and low in other large neutral amino
                               acids [66]. The Mediterranean diet, rich in fibre, B vitamins, magnesium, and zinc, has
                               been associated with improved sleep quality. In contrast, highly processed diets—high in
                               simple carbohydrates and saturated fats—may negatively affect sleep quality by promoting

                               high-GI meals can reduce sleep onset latency, suggesting a potential facilitation of sleep

                               highlighting the possibility of population-specific or context-dependent effects [68].

                               F. (2025) https://BioRender.com/f608i2g, (accessed on 20 October 2025).

                                    Caffeine consumption prior to or during competition is common in up to 90% of
                               athletes, establishing it as the most widely used psychoactive substance. Moss et al. showed
                               that higher caffeinated beverage intake was related to poorer sleep quality and increased
                               the risk for disordered breathing while sleeping among endurance athletes. Individuals
                               consuming 1.5 cups or fewer of caffeinated beverages per day reported better sleep quality,
                               as measured by the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire (ASSQ) global score, compared
                               to those athletes with higher levels of caffeine consumption [69].

                                    Athletes are particularly susceptible to ω-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) in-
                               sufficiency, a factor that should be considered in the development of their nutritional

                               primary dietary sources of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).
                               Plant-based sources of alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) include flaxseeds and flaxseed oil, chia
                               seeds, and walnuts. In cases where achieving sufficient dietary intake is difficult or im-
                               practical, appropriately dosed supplementation may be an effective approach. ω-3 PUFAs
                               play a vital role in maintaining optimal physiological functioning, influencing both overall

                               5.1. Sleep Deprivation and Athletic Performance
                                     Craven et al. completed a meta-analysis that highlighted the negative impact of sleep
                               deprivation and late sleep restriction on the physical performance of athletes. Sleep loss
                               was detrimental to the athletic performance both in the AM (ante meridiem) and PM
                               (post meridiem), but the outcome was worse in the PM. Anaerobic power, speed, and
                               power endurance, as well as high-intensity interval exercise, were all negatively affected by
                               disturbances in the sleep cycle [72].
                                     Sleep disorders change our physical performance. Hu et al. evaluated professional
                               Chinese winter sport athletes and revealed that 13% of the participants scored high for
                               symptoms of insomnia, while some demonstrated mental health problems [5]. Young
                               athletes can also experience related problems. A study documented poor sleep quality
                               (PSQI ≥ 5) concerns in 61.1% and 63.8% of the under-14 (U14) and under-17 (U17) partici-
                               pants, respectively, while 8.3% of the U14 and 8.4% of the U17 presented mild insomnia [73].
                               Craven et al. demonstrated that acute sleep loss, defined as ≤ 6 h of sleep within any 24 h,
                               negatively affected strength, anaerobic power/capacity, endurance, and skill-based activi-
                               ties. Sleep loss had a significant (p = 0.001) impact on performance outcomes. Total sleep
                               deprivation and late sleep restriction protocols were associated with the most pronounced
                               declines across various exercise modalities. Meta-regression analyses revealed that exercise
                               performance decreased by approximately 0.4% for every additional hour spent awake
                               following sleep loss. Based on these findings, physical activity after sleep loss should be
                               scheduled as early as possible to minimise performance impairments [72]. Brotherton et al.
                               demonstrated that performance in maximal grip and bench press (reduction in average
                               power, average force, and peak velocity), as well as submaximal leg press values (average

                               Gallagher et al., who found that implementing a 30—or 60-min nap at 1:00 PM after two

                               et al. [76] demonstrated that a daytime nap lasting between 30 and <60 min had a positive
                               effect on physical performance, including strength, endurance, and speed, following partial
                               sleep deprivation, as well as after regular sleep. Moreover, physical performance improved
                               progressively over time after the nap. Therefore, a minimum interval of 60 min post-nap
                               may be necessary to reduce the negative effects of sleep inertia.

                               function and reduced fatigue [76]. Napping affects not only athletes after sleep deprivation
                               but also after normal nighttime sleep. In the meta-analysis by Boukhris et al., napping
                               prior to afternoon training sessions showed a positive impact on performance outcomes.

                               inertia, and exercise type. Boukhris et al. showed that daytime napping improves perfor-

                               demonstrated that acute sleep deprivation significantly (p < 0.001) affects overall sporting

                               the performance parameters most susceptible to the negative effects of sleep deprivation

                               exertion, explosive power, and maximal strength. The type of sleep deprivation affected

                               that short-term sleep deprivation did not have a significant impact on anaerobic endurance

                               than non-athletes [79].

                               improved performance in tasks requiring gross motor skills (e.g., vertical jumps, maximal
                               sprints, or constant power output tests). Furthermore, analysis of specific sleep stages
                               indicated that spending less time in light sleep was linked to enhanced motor performance,
                               whereas time spent in deep sleep and REM sleep was not significantly associated with
                               gross motor skill outcomes [80].

                               aspects of physical performance. Depending on the sport discipline, extending nocturnal
                               sleep or napping can improve cognitive function (e.g., reaction time and shooting accuracy),
                               reduce daytime sleepiness, and enhance mood. Total sleep time required to achieve these
                               benefits may vary and should be established on a case-by-case basis. Sleep hygiene in
                               athletes can improve self-reported performance and facilitate training routine adjustment;
                               however, studies often do not provide sufficient details about the implemented sleep hy-
                               giene protocols, and post-exercise recovery strategies are even less conclusive, highlighting
                               the need for further research [81]. Sleep extension can improve sprint times, tennis serve
                               accuracy, swim turn and kick stroke efficiency, swim sprint, basketball shooting accuracy,
                               half-court and full-court sprints, and time to exhaustion. Enhanced cognitive function
                               can include reaction times, psychomotor vigilance tasks, alertness, vigour, and mood.

                               the effects of sleep restriction after evening exercise and observed a performance decline in

859	                               also leading to increased lactate accumulation and elevated cortisol levels. Concurrently,
860	                               muscle glycogen concentration decreases, and the ability to restore glycogen stores is im-
861	                               paired. Furthermore, sleep restriction can reduce anaerobic power, tennis serving accuracy,
862	                               isometric force, and average sprint times. Submaximal-effort sports are more vulnerable to
863	                               the negative consequences of sleep loss than maximum-effort sports. Prolonged periods of
864	                               sleep restriction are associated with increased sympathetic nervous system activity and
865	                               reduced parasympathetic activity, which may promote an overreaching or overtraining
866	                               state. In summary, these physiological disruptions may lead to a faster onset of exhaustion
867	                               during physical effort [34]. Smithies et al. evaluated a group of “elite cognitive performers”
868	                               (including pilots, air traffic controllers, surgeons, medical residents, emergency respon-
869	                               ders, process operators, and athletes) and observed that sleep loss impairs performance
870	                               on monotonous, low-salience tasks. In contrast, the ability to perform more complex and
871	                               cognitively stable tasks was relatively preserved. Sleep restriction may thus affect tasks
872	                               requiring rapid strategic shifts or responsiveness to varied stimuli, potentially compro-
873	                               mising adaptive decision-making in dynamic environments [89]. Total sleep deprivation,
874	                               partial sleep restriction, and sleep fragmentation negatively affect emotional functioning in
875	                               healthy individuals, as evidenced by reduced positive affect, increased anxiety symptoms,
876	                               and diminished emotional reactivity [90].
877	
878	                               5.2. Sleep Disorders (SD)
879	                                     Sleep disorders are a heterogeneous group of conditions that disrupt sleep and are di-
880	                               agnosed, for example, using PSG and ACG. They include: insomnia (ID)—chronic difficulty
881	                               falling asleep or maintaining sleep (up to 12.4% of the population) associated with psy-
882	                               chological and genetic factors [91–97]; type 1 narcolepsy—autoimmune damage to orexin
883	                               neurons causing excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy [98–100]; NREM parasomnias
884	                               (sleepwalking, night terrors)—disturbances in the NREM-wake transition with motor and
885	                               autonomic symptoms, partially genetically determined [101–103]; obstructive sleep apnoea
886	                               (OSA)—collapse of the upper airways during sleep, often associated with obesity [104,105];
887	                               and restless legs syndrome (RLS)—an urge to move the legs that intensifies at rest, more
888	                               common with iron deficiency [106–108]. Both short (<7 h) and long (>9 h) sleep increase
889	                               the risk of mortality and cardiovascular diseases [109]; ID and OSA are strongly associated
890	                               with autonomic dysfunction, metabolic disturbances, and inflammation [110]. Circadian
891	                               rhythm disorders contribute to heart disease and worsen prognosis in infections [111,112],
892	                               while ID more than doubles the risk of depression [113,114].
893	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                              19 of 43
894	
895

897	                                     Sleep deficiency and poor sleep quality (≤7 h/night, fragmentation) are common in
898	                               athletes and have numerous negative consequences: they impair physical and cognitive
899	                               performance, prolong recovery, reduce immunity, increase injury risk (in youth, ≤8 h
900	                               of sleep increases injury risk by 1.7 times); in adolescents, sleep deprivation strongly
901	                               correlates with musculoskeletal injuries, while prolonged sleep disturbances increase injury
902	                               risk; in elite and youth athletes, SD is common, often exceeding 50%, and is associated
903	                               with poorer mental health. Sleep monitoring (e.g., interviews, actigraphy, behavioural
904	                               therapy, sleep hygiene) should thus become part of injury prevention, training, and health
905	                               optimisation [115].
906	
907	                               5.3. Sleep Disturbances as a Risk of Other Diseases
908	                                     Sleep disturbances in athletes have been increasingly recognised not only as
909	                               performance-limiting factors but also as significant contributors to broader health risks. In-
910	                               adequate sleep duration and poor sleep quality are independently associated with increased
911	                               risks of musculoskeletal injuries, impaired cognitive functioning, mood disturbances, and
912	                               delayed recovery processes in athletes [34]. High-quality sleep supports sustained focus
913	                               and psychological stability during competition, potentially enhancing athletic performance.
914	                               Additionally, it plays a crucial role in post-exercise recovery processes, thereby reducing
915	                               the risk of injury and contributing to the prolongation of athletic careers [35]. Importantly,
916	                               sleep-disordered breathing, particularly obstructive sleep apnoea, has been identified as a
917	                               potential, underdiagnosed cause of sudden cardiac death during physical exertion in ath-
918	                               letes, underscoring the cardiovascular risks associated with untreated sleep disorders [116].
919	                               Sleep deficiency promotes metabolic disturbances by affecting carbohydrate metabolism
920	                               and the regulation of the expression level of appetite-related hormones, which may increase
921	                               the risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes. This consequently reduces athletic performance
922	                               and leads to long-term health complications [117]. Sleep disorders also negatively impact
923	                               immune system function, decreasing immunity and prolonging recovery time following
924	                               injuries or infections [118]. Collectively, chronic sleep disruption in athletes not only affects
925	                               performance but promotes a multidimensional health threat that warrants routine screen-
926	                               ing, education, and targeted intervention as part of comprehensive sports medicine and
927	                               training programs.
928	                                     Total or partial sleep deprivation reduces physical performance, strength, power,
929	                               and endurance, increases cortisol levels, lowers testosterone, and contributes to injuries
930	                               and mood disturbances, especially in young athletes. High-quality sleep, sleep extension,
931	                               and short naps improve recovery, reaction time, technical precision, and delay fatigue.
932	                               Sleep disorders, jet lag, and unfavorable dietary habits intensify fatigue, weaken immunity
933	                               and concentration, while a proper diet supports circadian rhythm and sleep quality. The
934	                               negative consequences of sleep deprivation, circadian rhythm disruptions, and sleep disor-
935	                               ders, leading to reduced performance and an increased risk of injuries, are presented in
936	                               Table 2 [64–90,104–115].

991	                               6. Treatment of Sleep Disorders in Athletes
992	                                    Pharmacological treatment of sleep disturbances in athletes entails numerous chal-
993	                               lenges and limitations, particularly in the context of anti-doping regulations governing elite
994	                               sports. Several sedative and hypnotic medications are included in the World Anti-Doping
995	                               Agency’s (WADA) list of prohibited substances or are subject to special usage restrictions,
996	                               including benzodiazepines and certain “Z-drugs” such as zolpidem. Although effective
997	                               in managing insomnia, these agents can impair cognitive functions, reaction time, and
998	                               psychomotor performance. Consequently, at higher doses, they are classified as substances
999	                               with proven abuse potential [119].
1000	                                    Zolpidem, while not explicitly prohibited by WADA, has raised concerns due to the
1001	                               risk of dependency and adverse side effects, especially in elite athletic populations. Cases
1002	                               of misuse, often in combination with alcohol or other sedatives, have led to increased
1003	                               scrutiny of its use in sports settings [120]. Athletes using such medications must be aware
1004	                               that improper or excessive intake may adversely affect not only sleep quality but also
1005	                               performance, recovery, and decision-making capabilities.
1006	                                    Cannabinoids represent another class of substances relevant to the management of
1007	                               sleep. While the non-psychoactive compound cannabidiol (CBD) is legal and may offer
1008	                               benefits for sleep, tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive component of
1009	                               cannabis, remains prohibited in sports competitions. Its detection in biological samples
1010	                               may result in disqualification, irrespective of the intent or mode of administration [119,121].
1011	                               Furthermore, the dietary supplement market for CBD products is insufficiently regulated,
1012	                               leading to the potential for contamination with prohibited levels of THC.
1013	                                    Over-the-counter sleep-promoting supplements are also of concern as some products
1014	                               contain undeclared substances, including anabolic steroids or other psychoactive agents.

1022	                               a natural hormone that regulates the circadian rhythm. Melatonin supplementation has
1023	                               proven particularly effective in cases of delayed sleep phase syndrome, jet lag, and in
1024	                               athletes who train or compete during evening hours. It improves sleep quality without the

1026	                               drowsiness, impaired balance, or cognitive decline [123]. Importantly, melatonin is not
1027	                               included in the WADA Prohibited List and is considered safe for short-term use. Melatonin
1028	                               has neuroprotective and antioxidant properties, which may further benefit recovery in ath-
1029	                               letic populations [124]. Amongst pharmacological agents with sleep-promoting properties,
1030	                               certain antidepressants, particularly those with sedative profiles, have been recognised for
1031	                               their efficacy in managing sleep disturbances. According to current anti-doping regula-
1032	                               tions, the therapeutic use of antidepressant medications in athletes is not prohibited, and
1033	                               such treatment does not require a Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE) [119,125]. While the
1034	                               mechanisms through which these drugs modulate specific neurotransmitter systems in the
1035	                               central nervous system are well established, their effects on physical performance and ath-
1036	                               letic outcomes remain insufficiently investigated. Despite their widespread use in clinical
1037	                               practice, the implications of antidepressant therapy on exercise capacity and competitive
1038	                               performance in athletes have not been thoroughly investigated. This underscores the need
1039	                               for cautious and evidence-informed decision-making when considering these agents for
1040	                               sleep-related complaints in athletes [126].
1041	                                     Trazodone is a sedating antidepressant used for insomnia by blocking serotonin 5-
1042	                               HT2 A, alpha-1 adrenergic, and histamine H1 receptors, thereby facilitating sleep onset
1043	                               and maintenance. Although extensively studied in general populations, its safety and
1044	                               efficacy in elite athletes remain poorly defined with no controlled trials directly assessing its
1045	                               impact on performance, recovery, or exercise physiology [127,128]. In primary insomniacs,
1046	                               a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study administering 50 mg trazodone
1047	                               nightly for 7 days demonstrated improved sleep maintenance, increased slow-wave sleep,
1048	                               and reduced nocturnal awakenings, yet concurrently revealed next-day impairments in
1049	                               short-term memory, verbal learning, equilibrium, and arm muscle endurance [129,130].
1050	                               These findings suggest potential psychomotor and alertness decrements following tra-
1051	                               zodone use. Pharmacokinetic studies in healthy subjects comparing controlled-release
1052	                               versus conventional trazodone confirmed its sedative profile, with reductions in subjective
1053	                               alertness and prolonged reaction times. However, these investigations did not involve
1054	                               athletes nor an evaluation of performance under physical exertion [131].
1055	                                     The effects of mirtazapine, an antidepressant, on sleep efficiency have been evaluated
1056	                               in healthy adults and general clinical populations. However, no studies have investigated
1057	                               the use of mirtazapine for insomnia or sleep disturbances in athlete populations, nor its
1058	                               effects on athletic performance or recovery metrics.
1059	                                     A controlled trial in young healthy volunteers (30 mg single dose) demonstrated
1060	                               that mirtazapine significantly improved sleep efficiency, increased slow-wave sleep, and
1061	                               reduced nocturnal awakenings, without notable effects on REM sleep. However, side
1062	                               effects such as next-day drowsiness, psychomotor impairment, and delayed reaction time
1063	                               have been consistently reported, raising concerns about its use in populations requiring
1064	                               high-level cognitive and physical function [132]. In general practice, the randomised
1065	                               DREAMING trial evaluated a low-dose of mirtazapine (7.5–15 mg/day) in patients with
1066	                               insomnia disorder. The study observed a statistically significant improvement in insomnia
1067	                               severity at 6 weeks compared to the group that received a placebo, yet the effects were
1068	                               not sustained at 12 weeks or at the 12-month follow-up. The side effects were more
