1074	                               significant [133]. Although the sedative profile of mirtazapine poses potential risks for
1075	                               athletic performance, mainly impaired alertness and coordination, there is no conclusive
1076	                               data in the athletic context. Although mirtazapine is not prohibited by WADA [119],
1077	                               and its usage does not require a TUE [125], its application in athletes warrants careful
1078	                               clinical oversight.
1079	                                     Mianserin, a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA), mani-
1080	                               fests sedative effects via antagonism of histamine H1 and α2 -adrenergic receptors. These
1081	                               properties may facilitate sleep onset and extend sleep duration, yet the general sedative
1082	                               profile raises concerns in populations requiring high vigilance and physical performance.
1083	                               A randomised crossover study administering healthy volunteers mianserin (30–60 mg at
1084	                               night) over 16 days showed increased total sleep time and subjective restfulness. However,
1085	                               mild but considerable impairments in driving performance and psychomotor vigilance,
1086	                               especially early during treatment, persisted through day 16, indicating incomplete tolerance
1087	                               development [134]. Although mianserin is not listed on the WADA Prohibited List [119]
1088	                               and its use does not require a TUE [125], there are no studies evaluating its use in athlete
1089	                               populations, nor data on its impact on training metrics and recovery. Nevertheless, due to
1090	                               potential sedation, delayed reaction times, and psychomotor slowing, its use in athletes
1091	                               demands careful clinical oversight. Given the absence of specific evidence and the docu-
1092	                               mented psychomotor effects, routine use of mianserin in sports medicine practice for sleep
1093	                               disorders is not advisable. Its administration may be considered only when behavioural
1094	                               and environmental interventions have failed, and using the lowest effective dose, with
1095	                               close monitoring of adverse effects and functional performance.
1096	                                     From a clinical standpoint, pharmacological treatment in athletes of sleep disorders
1097	                               should be reserved for clearly defined medical indications and applied with caution. In
1098	                               such cases, the issuance of a TUE may be necessary. Chemical agents with a short half-
1099	                               life and low potential for dependency are preferred, and pharmacotherapy should be
1100	                               time-limited and closely monitored.
1101	                                     Teams should engage in systematic evaluation of sleep patterns and the daily routines
1102	                               of their athletes. Maintaining sleep and recovery logs can be a valuable tool for tracking
1103	                               changes in rest quality and assessing their impact on athletic performance. It is also
1104	                               essential to regularly review both home and travel schedules, with particular attention
1105	                               to their potential effects on sleep. Fostering a team culture that prioritises and supports
1106	                               healthy sleep practices should be a foundational element. Developing individualised
1107	                               sleep plans tailored to the physiological needs and circadian preferences of each athlete is
1108	                               recommended. In selected cases, the implementation of objective sleep monitoring tools
1109	                               may be beneficial. Additionally, athletes should be evaluated for common sleep disorders,
1110	                               such as insomnia or obstructive sleep apnoea [135].

1210	                               7. Recovery Through Sleep in Athletes
1211	                                    Adequate sleep is a fundamental determinant of recovery, cognitive functioning, and
1212	                               injury prevention in athletes, with specific requirements varying according to the physio-
1213	                               logical and psychological demands of different sport disciplines. Optimal sleep duration,
1214	                               structured napping protocols, and consistent sleep hygiene routines are complemented
1215	                               by tailored recovery strategies such as thermal interventions, psychological skills training,
1216	                               and relaxation techniques. Overall, the reviewed strategies consistently emphasize the
1217	                               need for sufficient nocturnal sleep (typically 8–10 h, with longer durations during intensive
1218	                               training), the use of short, early-afternoon naps to support recovery and alertness, and
1219	                               the maintenance of stable circadian-aligned routines. Core recommendations also include
1220	                               limiting evening exposure to stimulants and electronic devices, optimizing the sleep en-
1221	                               vironment (cool, dark, and quiet), and incorporating structured recovery modalities such
1222	                               as foam rolling, cold- or heat-based therapies, and psychological techniques (relaxation,
1223	                               mindfulness, imagery, and breathing exercises). Collectively, these approaches aim to
1224	                               enhance sleep quality, accelerate recovery, and sustain both physical and cognitive per-
1225	                               formance across athletic populations [61,63,76,82,136–150]. Table 4 provides an overview
1226	                               of these evidence-based recommendations, highlighting both general and sport-specific
1227	                               considerations across endurance, strength, precision/technical, combat/fighting, and team
1228	                               sports.

1330	                               8. Discussion
1331	                                     According to the International Olympic Committee (IOC), sleep is a major contributor
1332	                               to athletic performance and a fundamental feature of athlete mental health [150]. Adequate
1333	                               sleep is crucial for optimal recovery and subsequent performance in athletes [81]. Adequate
1334	                               sleep has been shown to have restorative effects on the immune system and endocrine
1335	                               system, facilitate nervous system recovery and the metabolic cost of wakefulness, and
1336	                               play a significant role in learning, memory, and synaptic plasticity, which can affect sports
1337	                               recovery, injury risk reduction, and performance [151]. Athletes who sleep adequately
1338	                               before competition are likely to benefit from the standpoint of peak performance [82]. For
1339	                               elite athletes who exercise at a high level, sleep is critical to overall health, general well-
1340	                               being and performance. Sleep is therefore as important as exercise routine and diet [82].
1341	                               Research indicates that professional athletes should increase their sleep time. Athletes need
1342	                               9–10 h of total sleep time to reach their full potential [82,152]. The need to extend sleep time
1343	                               stems from the physical and psychological demands of the sport [115]. However, numerous
1344	                               studies have also reported that athletes frequently fail to achieve the recommended 7–9 h
1345	                               of sleep because of both sport-related and external factors, thereby compromising the
1346	                               quality of their recovery [7]. Restoration of sleep and sleep extension are crucial for
1347	                               athletes to recover from exhaustion [153]. Improving sleep resulted in decreased fatigue
1348	                               and sleepiness [154]. Sleep extension (bank sleep) may bring potential benefits such as
1349	                               improving athletic performance and mood, reducing stress levels, and alleviating anxiety
1350	                               associated with participating in an important competition. By getting more sleep before an

                               Additionally, sleep loss can harm muscle endurance and performance of military-specific

                                    Sleep deprivation negatively affects physical performance in athletes, although results
                               remain inconclusive due to substantial variability in study protocols and experimental
                               designs. Sleep restriction alters heart rate, ventilation, and respiratory frequency, while
                               also leading to increased lactate accumulation and elevated cortisol levels. Concurrently,
                               muscle glycogen concentration decreases, and the ability to restore glycogen stores is im-
                               paired. Furthermore, sleep restriction can reduce anaerobic power, tennis serving accuracy,
                               isometric force, and average sprint times. Submaximal-effort sports are more vulnerable to
                               the negative consequences of sleep loss than maximum-effort sports. Prolonged periods of
                               sleep restriction are associated with increased sympathetic nervous system activity and
                               reduced parasympathetic activity, which may promote an overreaching or overtraining
                               state. In summary, these physiological disruptions may lead to a faster onset of exhaustion
                               during physical effort [34]. Smithies et al. evaluated a group of “elite cognitive performers”
                               (including pilots, air traffic controllers, surgeons, medical residents, emergency respon-
                               ders, process operators, and athletes) and observed that sleep loss impairs performance
                               on monotonous, low-salience tasks. In contrast, the ability to perform more complex and
                               cognitively stable tasks was relatively preserved. Sleep restriction may thus affect tasks
                               requiring rapid strategic shifts or responsiveness to varied stimuli, potentially compro-
                               mising adaptive decision-making in dynamic environments [89]. Total sleep deprivation,
                               partial sleep restriction, and sleep fragmentation negatively affect emotional functioning in
                               healthy individuals, as evidenced by reduced positive affect, increased anxiety symptoms,
                               and diminished emotional reactivity [90].

                               5.2. Sleep Disorders (SD)
                                     Sleep disorders are a heterogeneous group of conditions that disrupt sleep and are di-
                               agnosed, for example, using PSG and ACG. They include: insomnia (ID)—chronic difficulty
                               falling asleep or maintaining sleep (up to 12.4% of the population) associated with psy-
                               chological and genetic factors [91–97]; type 1 narcolepsy—autoimmune damage to orexin
                               neurons causing excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy [98–100]; NREM parasomnias
                               (sleepwalking, night terrors)—disturbances in the NREM-wake transition with motor and
                               autonomic symptoms, partially genetically determined [101–103]; obstructive sleep apnoea
                               (OSA)—collapse of the upper airways during sleep, often associated with obesity [104,105];
                               and restless legs syndrome (RLS)—an urge to move the legs that intensifies at rest, more
                               common with iron deficiency [106–108]. Both short (<7 h) and long (>9 h) sleep increase
                               the risk of mortality and cardiovascular diseases [109]; ID and OSA are strongly associated
                               with autonomic dysfunction, metabolic disturbances, and inflammation [110]. Circadian
                               rhythm disorders contribute to heart disease and worsen prognosis in infections [111,112],
                               while ID more than doubles the risk of depression [113,114].

                                     Sleep deficiency and poor sleep quality (≤7 h/night, fragmentation) are common in
                               athletes and have numerous negative consequences: they impair physical and cognitive
                               performance, prolong recovery, reduce immunity, increase injury risk (in youth, ≤8 h
                               of sleep increases injury risk by 1.7 times); in adolescents, sleep deprivation strongly
                               correlates with musculoskeletal injuries, while prolonged sleep disturbances increase injury
                               risk; in elite and youth athletes, SD is common, often exceeding 50%, and is associated
                               with poorer mental health. Sleep monitoring (e.g., interviews, actigraphy, behavioural
                               therapy, sleep hygiene) should thus become part of injury prevention, training, and health
                               optimisation [115].

                               5.3. Sleep Disturbances as a Risk of Other Diseases
                                     Sleep disturbances in athletes have been increasingly recognised not only as
                               performance-limiting factors but also as significant contributors to broader health risks. In-
                               adequate sleep duration and poor sleep quality are independently associated with increased
                               risks of musculoskeletal injuries, impaired cognitive functioning, mood disturbances, and
                               delayed recovery processes in athletes [34]. High-quality sleep supports sustained focus
                               and psychological stability during competition, potentially enhancing athletic performance.
                               Additionally, it plays a crucial role in post-exercise recovery processes, thereby reducing
                               the risk of injury and contributing to the prolongation of athletic careers [35]. Importantly,
                               sleep-disordered breathing, particularly obstructive sleep apnoea, has been identified as a
                               potential, underdiagnosed cause of sudden cardiac death during physical exertion in ath-
                               letes, underscoring the cardiovascular risks associated with untreated sleep disorders [116].
                               Sleep deficiency promotes metabolic disturbances by affecting carbohydrate metabolism
                               and the regulation of the expression level of appetite-related hormones, which may increase
                               the risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes. This consequently reduces athletic performance
                               and leads to long-term health complications [117]. Sleep disorders also negatively impact
                               immune system function, decreasing immunity and prolonging recovery time following
                               injuries or infections [118]. Collectively, chronic sleep disruption in athletes not only affects
                               performance but promotes a multidimensional health threat that warrants routine screen-
                               ing, education, and targeted intervention as part of comprehensive sports medicine and
                               training programs.
                                     Total or partial sleep deprivation reduces physical performance, strength, power,
                               and endurance, increases cortisol levels, lowers testosterone, and contributes to injuries
                               and mood disturbances, especially in young athletes. High-quality sleep, sleep extension,
                               and short naps improve recovery, reaction time, technical precision, and delay fatigue.
                               Sleep disorders, jet lag, and unfavorable dietary habits intensify fatigue, weaken immunity
                               and concentration, while a proper diet supports circadian rhythm and sleep quality. The

                               6. Treatment of Sleep Disorders in Athletes
                                    Pharmacological treatment of sleep disturbances in athletes entails numerous chal-
                               lenges and limitations, particularly in the context of anti-doping regulations governing elite
                               sports. Several sedative and hypnotic medications are included in the World Anti-Doping
                               Agency’s (WADA) list of prohibited substances or are subject to special usage restrictions,
                               including benzodiazepines and certain “Z-drugs” such as zolpidem. Although effective
                               in managing insomnia, these agents can impair cognitive functions, reaction time, and
                               psychomotor performance. Consequently, at higher doses, they are classified as substances
                               with proven abuse potential [119].
                                    Zolpidem, while not explicitly prohibited by WADA, has raised concerns due to the
                               risk of dependency and adverse side effects, especially in elite athletic populations. Cases
                               of misuse, often in combination with alcohol or other sedatives, have led to increased
                               scrutiny of its use in sports settings [120]. Athletes using such medications must be aware
                               that improper or excessive intake may adversely affect not only sleep quality but also
                               performance, recovery, and decision-making capabilities.
                                    Cannabinoids represent another class of substances relevant to the management of
                               sleep. While the non-psychoactive compound cannabidiol (CBD) is legal and may offer
                               benefits for sleep, tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive component of
                               cannabis, remains prohibited in sports competitions. Its detection in biological samples
                               may result in disqualification, irrespective of the intent or mode of administration [119,121].
                               Furthermore, the dietary supplement market for CBD products is insufficiently regulated,
                               leading to the potential for contamination with prohibited levels of THC.
                                    Over-the-counter sleep-promoting supplements are also of concern as some products
                               contain undeclared substances, including anabolic steroids or other psychoactive agents.
 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                            21 of 43



                               This presents a serious risk of inadvertent doping violations amongst athletes who may
                               unknowingly consume contaminated supplements [122].
                                     Melatonin is a legal substance, frequently employed to support sleep in athletes, and
                               a natural hormone that regulates the circadian rhythm. Melatonin supplementation has
                               proven particularly effective in cases of delayed sleep phase syndrome, jet lag, and in
                               athletes who train or compete during evening hours. It improves sleep quality without the
                               adverse effects commonly associated with pharmacological hypnotics, such as daytime
                               drowsiness, impaired balance, or cognitive decline [123]. Importantly, melatonin is not
                               included in the WADA Prohibited List and is considered safe for short-term use. Melatonin
                               has neuroprotective and antioxidant properties, which may further benefit recovery in ath-
                               letic populations [124]. Amongst pharmacological agents with sleep-promoting properties,
                               certain antidepressants, particularly those with sedative profiles, have been recognised for
                               their efficacy in managing sleep disturbances. According to current anti-doping regula-
                               tions, the therapeutic use of antidepressant medications in athletes is not prohibited, and
                               such treatment does not require a Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE) [119,125]. While the
                               mechanisms through which these drugs modulate specific neurotransmitter systems in the
                               central nervous system are well established, their effects on physical performance and ath-
                               letic outcomes remain insufficiently investigated. Despite their widespread use in clinical
                               practice, the implications of antidepressant therapy on exercise capacity and competitive
                               performance in athletes have not been thoroughly investigated. This underscores the need
                               for cautious and evidence-informed decision-making when considering these agents for
                               sleep-related complaints in athletes [126].
                                     Trazodone is a sedating antidepressant used for insomnia by blocking serotonin 5-
                               HT2 A, alpha-1 adrenergic, and histamine H1 receptors, thereby facilitating sleep onset
                               and maintenance. Although extensively studied in general populations, its safety and
                               efficacy in elite athletes remain poorly defined with no controlled trials directly assessing its
                               impact on performance, recovery, or exercise physiology [127,128]. In primary insomniacs,
                               a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study administering 50 mg trazodone
                               nightly for 7 days demonstrated improved sleep maintenance, increased slow-wave sleep,
                               and reduced nocturnal awakenings, yet concurrently revealed next-day impairments in
                               short-term memory, verbal learning, equilibrium, and arm muscle endurance [129,130].
                               These findings suggest potential psychomotor and alertness decrements following tra-
                               zodone use. Pharmacokinetic studies in healthy subjects comparing controlled-release
                               versus conventional trazodone confirmed its sedative profile, with reductions in subjective
                               alertness and prolonged reaction times. However, these investigations did not involve
                               athletes nor an evaluation of performance under physical exertion [131].
                                     The effects of mirtazapine, an antidepressant, on sleep efficiency have been evaluated
                               in healthy adults and general clinical populations. However, no studies have investigated
                               the use of mirtazapine for insomnia or sleep disturbances in athlete populations, nor its
                               effects on athletic performance or recovery metrics.
                                     A controlled trial in young healthy volunteers (30 mg single dose) demonstrated
                               that mirtazapine significantly improved sleep efficiency, increased slow-wave sleep, and
                               reduced nocturnal awakenings, without notable effects on REM sleep. However, side
                               effects such as next-day drowsiness, psychomotor impairment, and delayed reaction time
                               have been consistently reported, raising concerns about its use in populations requiring
                               high-level cognitive and physical function [132]. In general practice, the randomised
                               DREAMING trial evaluated a low-dose of mirtazapine (7.5–15 mg/day) in patients with
                               insomnia disorder. The study observed a statistically significant improvement in insomnia
                               severity at 6 weeks compared to the group that received a placebo, yet the effects were
                               not sustained at 12 weeks or at the 12-month follow-up. The side effects were more
 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                        22 of 43



                               frequent with mirtazapine than those with the placebo, although the differences were not
                               significant [133]. Although the sedative profile of mirtazapine poses potential risks for
                               athletic performance, mainly impaired alertness and coordination, there is no conclusive
                               data in the athletic context. Although mirtazapine is not prohibited by WADA [119],
                               and its usage does not require a TUE [125], its application in athletes warrants careful
                               clinical oversight.
                                     Mianserin, a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA), mani-
                               fests sedative effects via antagonism of histamine H1 and α2 -adrenergic receptors. These
                               properties may facilitate sleep onset and extend sleep duration, yet the general sedative
                               profile raises concerns in populations requiring high vigilance and physical performance.
                               A randomised crossover study administering healthy volunteers mianserin (30–60 mg at
                               night) over 16 days showed increased total sleep time and subjective restfulness. However,
                               mild but considerable impairments in driving performance and psychomotor vigilance,
                               especially early during treatment, persisted through day 16, indicating incomplete tolerance
                               development [134]. Although mianserin is not listed on the WADA Prohibited List [119]
                               and its use does not require a TUE [125], there are no studies evaluating its use in athlete
                               populations, nor data on its impact on training metrics and recovery. Nevertheless, due to
                               potential sedation, delayed reaction times, and psychomotor slowing, its use in athletes
                               demands careful clinical oversight. Given the absence of specific evidence and the docu-
                               mented psychomotor effects, routine use of mianserin in sports medicine practice for sleep
                               disorders is not advisable. Its administration may be considered only when behavioural
                               and environmental interventions have failed, and using the lowest effective dose, with
                               close monitoring of adverse effects and functional performance.
                                     From a clinical standpoint, pharmacological treatment in athletes of sleep disorders
                               should be reserved for clearly defined medical indications and applied with caution. In
                               such cases, the issuance of a TUE may be necessary. Chemical agents with a short half-
                               life and low potential for dependency are preferred, and pharmacotherapy should be
                               time-limited and closely monitored.
                                     Teams should engage in systematic evaluation of sleep patterns and the daily routines
                               of their athletes. Maintaining sleep and recovery logs can be a valuable tool for tracking
                               changes in rest quality and assessing their impact on athletic performance. It is also
                               essential to regularly review both home and travel schedules, with particular attention
                               to their potential effects on sleep. Fostering a team culture that prioritises and supports
                               healthy sleep practices should be a foundational element. Developing individualised
                               sleep plans tailored to the physiological needs and circadian preferences of each athlete is
                               recommended. In selected cases, the implementation of objective sleep monitoring tools
                               may be beneficial. Additionally, athletes should be evaluated for common sleep disorders,
                               such as insomnia or obstructive sleep apnoea [135].

                               7. Recovery Through Sleep in Athletes
                                    Adequate sleep is a fundamental determinant of recovery, cognitive functioning, and
                               injury prevention in athletes, with specific requirements varying according to the physio-
                               logical and psychological demands of different sport disciplines. Optimal sleep duration,
                               structured napping protocols, and consistent sleep hygiene routines are complemented
                               by tailored recovery strategies such as thermal interventions, psychological skills training,
                               and relaxation techniques. Overall, the reviewed strategies consistently emphasize the
                               need for sufficient nocturnal sleep (typically 8–10 h, with longer durations during intensive
                               training), the use of short, early-afternoon naps to support recovery and alertness, and
                               the maintenance of stable circadian-aligned routines. Core recommendations also include
                               limiting evening exposure to stimulants and electronic devices, optimizing the sleep en-
                               vironment (cool, dark, and quiet), and incorporating structured recovery modalities such
                               as foam rolling, cold- or heat-based therapies, and psychological techniques (relaxation,
                               mindfulness, imagery, and breathing exercises). Collectively, these approaches aim to
                               enhance sleep quality, accelerate recovery, and sustain both physical and cognitive per-
                               formance across athletic populations [61,63,76,82,136–150]. Table 4 provides an overview
                               of these evidence-based recommendations, highlighting both general and sport-specific
                               considerations across endurance, strength, precision/technical, combat/fighting, and team
                               sports.

                               8. Discussion
                                     According to the International Olympic Committee (IOC), sleep is a major contributor
                               to athletic performance and a fundamental feature of athlete mental health [150]. Adequate
                               sleep is crucial for optimal recovery and subsequent performance in athletes [81]. Adequate
                               sleep has been shown to have restorative effects on the immune system and endocrine
                               system, facilitate nervous system recovery and the metabolic cost of wakefulness, and
                               play a significant role in learning, memory, and synaptic plasticity, which can affect sports
                               recovery, injury risk reduction, and performance [151]. Athletes who sleep adequately
                               before competition are likely to benefit from the standpoint of peak performance [82]. For
                               elite athletes who exercise at a high level, sleep is critical to overall health, general well-
                               being and performance. Sleep is therefore as important as exercise routine and diet [82].
                               Research indicates that professional athletes should increase their sleep time. Athletes need
                               9–10 h of total sleep time to reach their full potential [82,152]. The need to extend sleep time
                               stems from the physical and psychological demands of the sport [115]. However, numerous
                               studies have also reported that athletes frequently fail to achieve the recommended 7–9 h
                               of sleep because of both sport-related and external factors, thereby compromising the
                               quality of their recovery [7]. Restoration of sleep and sleep extension are crucial for
                               athletes to recover from exhaustion [153]. Improving sleep resulted in decreased fatigue
                               and sleepiness [154]. Sleep extension (bank sleep) may bring potential benefits such as
                               improving athletic performance and mood, reducing stress levels, and alleviating anxiety

1351	                               important competition, athletes can have confidence knowing that a poor night’s sleep the
1352	                               night before competition should not affect their performance [115]. The results of a study
1353	                               by Schartz et al. suggest that a minimum of 1 week of increased sleep duration leads to
1354	                               improvements on a range of performance measures among sleep-deprived athletes [155].
1355	                                     Sleep in athletes forms the foundation of regenerative and adaptive processes, serving
1356	                               as a key factor influencing physical performance, mental health, and injury prevention. The
1357	                               average sleep duration for adults is 7–8 h per day [1]; however, the regenerative needs of
1358	                               athletes, particularly those engaging in intensive training, are often greater. Differences in
1359	                               sleep duration and quality depend on gender, age, and training environment [1], indicating
1360	                               that sleep strategies should be individualised rather than universal.
1361	                                     In our narrative review, we aimed to comprehensively show how sleep affects the
1362	                               health and athletic results of athletes. We have demonstrated that sleep is no longer
1363	                               perceived as a passive element of recovery, but as an active and essential process that is
1364	                               fundamental to health, well-being, and achieving peak athletic performance. As Vitale et al.
1365	                               aptly conclude, the old adage “you snooze, you lose” should, in the world of sports, be:
1366	                               “you snooze (more), you win.” These authors emphasize that ignoring sleep can nullify the
1367	                               benefits of physical activity [82].
1368	                                     Athletes, especially at the collegiate level, are a group particularly vulnerable to sleep
1369	                               deprivation. Studies, such as those conducted by Mah and colleagues, clearly indicate
1370	                               that student-athletes often experience poor quality and insufficient amounts of sleep [156].
1371	                               The reasons for this are complex and include intense training schedules, academic respon-
1372	                               sibilities, travel, and competition-related stress. The consequences of sleep deprivation
1373	                               for athletes are multidimensional and well-documented. They include impaired reaction
1374	                               time, decreased accuracy, reduced strength and endurance, and cognitive function deficits,
1375	                               such as decision-making [82]. Research confirms these observations in practice, showing,
1376	                               for example, that sleep restriction directly impairs maximal jump performance and joint
1377	                               coordination in elite athletes [157].
1378	                                     An additional factor is circadian rhythm disruption, often caused by traveling across
1379	                               time zones. This has a direct impact on performance, as observed in professional American
1380	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                           29 of 43
1381	
1382	
1383	
1384	                               football players [158]. The negative effects of travel, including fatigue and desynchro-
1385	                               nization of the biological clock, pose a serious challenge for athletes at every level of
1386	                               competition [63]. One of the most effective ways to counteract the negative effects of
1387	                               sleep deprivation is to consciously extend it. This strategy, known as sleep extension, has
1388	                               been the subject of numerous studies that have consistently shown its positive impact
1389	                               on athletic performance. A groundbreaking study by Mah et al. on collegiate basketball
1390	                               players [159] showed that extending sleep to a minimum of 10 h per night for 5–7 weeks
1391	                               brought tangible benefits. As also highlighted in the attached review article by Vitale et al.,
1392	                               the basketball players showed improved sprint speed and a significant increase in shooting
1393	                               accuracy—for both free throws and 3-pointers—by over 9% [82]. Moreover, the athletes
1394	                               reported improved mood and overall well-being [159].
1395	                                     These benefits are not limited to basketball. Similar effects have been observed in
1396	                               other disciplines. Extended sleep improved reaction time off the blocks, turn efficiency,
1397	                               and overall well-being in swimmers [160]. In collegiate tennis players, an improvement
1398	                               in serve accuracy was noted. As in other team sports, additional sleep brought perfor-
1399	                               mance benefits [161]. Even in ultra-triathlons, sleep duration correlated with performance
1400	                               outcomes [162].
1401	                                     Currently, a newer concept is “sleep loading,” which involves deliberately extending
1402	                               sleep before a period of planned sleep deprivation. A study on professional baseball
1403	                               players showed that this strategy improves reaction time in visual search tasks and reduces
1404	                               perceived fatigue [163].
1405	                                     Scientific evidence clearly indicates that education about sleep is a key element of
1406	                               training programs. Educational initiatives, such as those conducted at Stanford Univer-
1407	                               sity, yield positive, long-term effects [164]. The role of the entire staff—coaches, doctors,
1408	                               and physiotherapists—is crucial here, as they should collaborate on managing athletes’
1409	                               sleep [165].
1410	                                     In their review, Vitale et al. provide practical tips on sleep hygiene that athletes
1411	                               can implement. These include maintaining regular waking and sleeping times, creating
1412	                               an optimal sleep environment (dark, quiet, cool room), avoiding stimulants (caffeine)
1413	                               and exposure to blue light from screens before bed, and introducing relaxing bedtime
1414	                               rituals [82].
1415	                                     Research shows that sleep deprivation in athletes leads to significant reductions in
1416	                               strength, power, endurance, and cognitive function, increasing the risk of injury, especially
1417	                               among younger athletes [5]. At the cellular level, sleep regulates immune and hormonal
1418	                               function as well as inflammatory cytokines, supporting post-exercise recovery and train-
1419	                               ing adaptations [4]. Additionally, epigenetic mechanisms, such as DNA methylation and
1420	                               microRNAs, may modulate the physiological response to training [6]. High-quality and ad-
1421	                               equately long sleep thus acts as a natural “regeneration window”, promoting performance
1422	                               gains and reducing oxidative stress [7].
1423	                                     One of the major challenges for athletes is the frequent travel across time zones, which
1424	                               leads to circadian desynchronisation and jet lag symptoms. In practice, this manifests
1425	                               as sleep disturbances, decreased concentration, irritability, fatigue, and gastrointestinal
1426	                               issues, all of which impair both physical and mental performance [60,61]. The direction of
1427	                               travel also plays a critical role—east–west travel presents greater challenges for circadian
1428	                               adjustment, whereas westward travel may result in competitions coinciding with the
1429	                               biological night of the athlete [61]. The consequences of circadian disruption are discipline-
1430	                               specific: endurance athletes generally require more sleep than strength athletes, and sleep
1431	                               deficits can significantly impair training effectiveness and competition performance [156].
1432	                                     From a psychological perspective, sleep and stress are closely interconnected. Chronic
1433	                               stress increases cortisol secretion, weakens immunity, and impairs recovery, while sleep
1434	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                            30 of 43
1435	
1436	
1437	
1438	                               deficits negatively affect cognitive function and concentration [166,167]. Interdisciplinary
1439	                               strategies, including psychoeducation, lifestyle optimisation, physiological monitoring, and
1440	                               social support, can reduce allostatic load, while metacognitive techniques, pre-performance
1441	                               routines, and relaxation support can increase regulation and psychological resilience.
1442	                               The effectiveness of these methods, however, depends on the experience, sport-specific
1443	                               demands, and individualised program design [166,167].
1444	                                     Napping interventions aim to increase the amount of sleep obtained via total sleep
1445	                               duration or brief targeted naps [152]. Daytime sleep quantity (naps) can supplement
1446	                               insufficient nighttime sleep, as well as being beneficial for people who want a boost in
1447	                               alertness [115]. A systematic review conducted by Bonnar et al. found that naps taken later
1448	                               in the day and at an appropriately timed interval after previous exercise may positively
1449	                               influence an athlete’s mental disposition towards subsequent performance tasks. However,
1450	                               a 20-min nap may be too short to influence subsequent performance measures among
1451	                               partially sleep-deprived athletes. It may also disturb sleep on the subsequent night for
1452	                               some athletes [81].
1453	                                     It is worth noting that athletes often face challenges such as travel, late-night games,
1454	                               and pool lane hours, which make it difficult to maintain a regular sleep schedule during
1455	                               certain times. In this context, it is important for those working with athletes to seek alter-
1456	                               native strategies aimed at ensuring healthy sleep in specific circumstances and conditions
1457	                               (such as choosing appropriate nap times or preparing an individual’s body clock for travel
1458	                               across time zones [81]. Recommendations for improving sleep also include taking into
1459	                               account individual chronotypes (evening vs. morning chronotype), i.e., avoiding training
1460	                               times early in the morning and late at night, depending on the individual preferences
1461	                               of athletes [115]. Chronotype is a significant variable in determining optimal times for
1462	                               training and competition. It may influence an athlete’s choice of sport or their success in it.
1463	                                     The importance of sleep education should also be emphasised, which consists of pro-
1464	                               viding adequate informational support (knowledge about sleep hygiene) and instrumental
1465	                               support (specific tips to help develop healthy sleep habits). Promoting sleep information
1466	                               specific to the athlete’s sport, such as sleep needs, adjusting to training times and em-
1467	                               phasising the impact of sleep on performance, is key to creating buy-in and behavioural
1468	                               change [115].
1469	                                     In addition to behavioural strategies aimed at developing healthy sleep habits, cog-
1470	                               nitive strategies are also used in working with athletes to reduce tension associated with
1471	                               anxiety and fear before competitions. Interventions involve identifying dysfunctional
1472	                               thoughts and seeking alternative solutions/scenarios, including progressive muscle re-
1473	                               laxation and meditation. Battaglini et al. documented that progressive muscle relaxation
1474	                               effectively reduces cognitive anxiety and stress related to sports (competitions, trips, and
1475	                               overtraining), lowers heart rate, and promotes the athlete’s recovery [168]. Anderson et al.
1476	                               recognised the validity of using mindfulness as an intervention aimed at improving athlete
1477	                               health and performance [169]. Vveinhardt et al. determined that mindfulness practices are
1478	                               related to athletes’ higher performance and better psycho-emotional state. The psychologi-
1479	                               cal state indicators of kyokushin athletes who used mindfulness techniques (meditation,
1480	                               concentration) were better than those of athletes who did not use these techniques and
1481	                               were unaware of the benefits of mindfulness [170]. The benefits of meditation experience
1482	                               in mitigating the negative effects of mental fatigue have been documented in studies by
1483	                               Nien et al. [171]. Other studies have shown that after 20-week mindfulness meditation
1484	                               training interventions, male fencer athletes exhibited lower salivary cortisol concentrations
1485	                               and mental fatigue [172].
1486	                                     Sleep problems in athletes are related to both sport-specific factors (high training loads,
1487	                               travel, and stress associated with competition) and non-sport factors [115]. In the case of
1488	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                         31 of 43
1489	
1490	
1491	
1492	                               non-sport-related factors, it may be necessary to refer to various forms of psychological
1493	                               assistance (crisis intervention, psychoeducation or psychotherapy).
1494	                                     Pharmacological interventions for sleep disorders in athletes present a nuanced risk-
1495	                               benefit calculus. Hypnotics and sedative antidepressants may improve sleep, but often at
1496	                               the expense of cognitive and physical performance, while legal alternatives like melatonin
1497	                               may offer safer, if modest, benefits. These realities underscore the need for individualised
1498	                               strategies, close monitoring, and integration with behavioural and environmental interven-
1499	                               tions. The ultimate goal is to enhance recovery and sleep quality without undermining
1500	                               athletic performance or violating anti-doping rules. Pharmacological hypnotics, such as
1501	                               benzodiazepines or “Z-drugs” like zolpidem, can improve insomnia, yet the risks for
1502	                               athletes are notable. On one hand, they can facilitate faster sleep onset and longer dura-
1503	                               tion; on the other hand, they impair reaction time, psychomotor function, and cognitive
1504	                               performance that are critical during training and competition [119,120]. Even when not
1505	                               explicitly prohibited by WADA, such as zolpidem, drugs carry dependency risks and may
1506	                               reduce next-day performance. From a practical standpoint, the potential gains in sleep may
1507	                               be offset by the declines in precision, coordination, or decision-making—core elements of
1508	                               athletic success.
1509	                                     Cannabinoids illustrate another grey area. While CBD appears safe and may sup-
1510	                               port sleep, THC is a banned drug, and supplement contamination is common [119,121].
1511	                               Therefore, athletes attempting a seemingly harmless intervention could face inadvertent
1512	                               doping violations. Over-the-counter sleep aids pose a similar dilemma, with undeclared
1513	                               psychoactive or anabolic substances potentially compromising the eligibility of the athlete
1514	                               to compete [122]. Thus, what may seem like a simple sleep solution can have far-reaching
1515	                               consequences for elite athletes.
1516	                                     Melatonin, by contrast, provides a compelling argument for use in sport. Its benefits
1517	                               for circadian adjustment, jet lag, and evening training schedules are well-documented, and
1518	                               its neuroprotective and antioxidant properties may support recovery [123,124]. Melatonin
1519	                               is also a legal drug under WADA rules, making it a lower-risk option in competitive sports.
1520	                               Yet, the question remains whether its effects on sleep translate into measurable performance
1521	                               gains in elite athletes—a topic still under investigation.
1522	                                     Sedative antidepressants—such as trazodone, mirtazapine, and mianserin—offer
1523	                               another layer of complexity. Studies in non-athletes show improved slow-wave sleep
1524	                               and reduced nocturnal awakenings [129–134]. However, side effects such as next-day
1525	                               drowsiness, psychomotor slowing, and delayed reaction times pose potential threats to
1526	                               athletic performance. The absence of athlete-specific trials means these medications are
1527	                               used empirically rather than based on rigorous evidence. While permitted under anti-
1528	                               doping regulations and not requiring a TUE [119,125], their sedative effects necessitate
1529	                               cautious application and monitoring, and individualised dosing. In some cases, the risks of
1530	                               using these sedative antidepressants may outweigh the benefits, particularly for athletes
1531	                               competing in sports requiring rapid reflexes and fine motor control.
1532	                                     Sleep in athletes is a dynamic process that not only enables rest but also actively
1533	                               supports regeneration, training adaptation, psychological resilience, and injury prevention.
1534	                               Understanding its importance in the context of intensive training, travel, and psychological
1535	                               stress allows for the design of personalised strategies to improve sleep quality, which in
1536	                               practice translates into optimised athletic performance and long-term health.
1537	
1538	                               9. Strengths and Limitations of This Review
1539	                                    We provide a comprehensive and multidimensional review examining physiological
1540	                               (including molecular and hormonal) as well as dietary and pharmacological determinants
1541	                               affecting sleep in athletes. This allows us to present a wide spectrum of factors influencing
1542	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                           32 of 43
1543	
1544	
1545	
1546	                               sleep—from neurotransmitters (e.g., serotonin, GABA, orexin, melatonin) to metabolic
1547	                               and neuroendocrine mechanisms. Chronic partial sleep deprivation in athletes can lead
1548	                               to disturbances in carbohydrate metabolism and neuroendocrine function, which in turn
1549	                               result in adverse changes in appetite, food intake, and protein synthesis. These effects
1550	                               involve numerous signalling pathways and alter protein expression levels [173]. The in-
1551	                               depth review of these molecular pathways contributes to deepening our understanding of
1552	                               the physiological basis of the importance of sleep in physical performance.
1553	                                    We also highlight the link between sleep and the specificity of elite sport. We addressed
1554	                               not only the general restorative function of sleep (e.g., the role of slow-wave sleep in
1555	                               repair processes) but also factors unique to athletes. The specific demands related to
1556	                               training, travel, competition, as well as sex and stress level—factors that significantly
1557	                               modulate sleep in athletes—are highlighted. Sport-specific factors (relating to training,
1558	                               travel, and competition) and non-sport factors (e.g., females, stress, and anxiety) can
1559	                               influence sleep in athletes [115]. This multidimensional perspective is consistent with
1560	                               the current approach to optimising sleep for athletes. For example, the International
1561	                               Olympic Committee (IOC) and National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) recognise
1562	                               healthy sleep as a fundamental component of health and performance and recommend
1563	                               individualised strategies for its improvement [34]. We therefore demonstrate alignment
1564	                               with the latest consensus statements and scientific findings.
1565	                                    It is worth noting the limitations of this review, including the generalised treatment of
1566	                               athletes as the homogeneous group. This simplification overlooks the fact that different
1567	                               sports impose different sleep demands. For example, studies have shown that American
1568	                               football (National Football League) players are more likely to experience obstructive sleep
1569	                               apnoea than other athletes or the general population. Similarly, endurance athletes may
1570	                               respond differently to sleep loss compared to sprinters or weightlifters. Such uniform
1571	                               categorisation diminishes nuances related to sport disciplines or training level [34].
1572	                                    Another drawback lies in the selective choice of factors affecting sleep. The review fo-
1573	                               cuses on classical determinants (such as dietary macronutrients and common supplements)
1574	                               and well-established neurochemical mechanisms, but omits less obvious yet potentially
1575	                               important aspects, such as a high-fibre diet—typical of the Mediterranean dietary pattern—
1576	                               investigated for its impact on sleep, associated with a significant increase in deep sleep
1577	                               at the expense of light sleep [174]. Excluding those diets, and despite evidence that fruit-,
1578	                               vegetable-, and whole grain–rich diets can improve sleep quality, is an example of selective
1579	                               variable inclusion. It is also worth emphasising that a high intake of fibre, particularly from
1580	                               whole grains, vegetables, and fruits, substantially increases meal volume and enhances
1581	                               satiety. Elevated energy requirements, typical of endurance sports, may lead to an unin-
1582	                               tentional reduction in total energy intake. Moreover, diets rich in fibre are characterised
1583	                               by low energy density, which further complicates meeting the caloric needs of female
1584	                               athletes. As a result, there is an increased risk of low energy availability (LEA), a condition
1585	                               associated with hormonal disturbances, reduced bone mineral density, and impaired recov-
1586	                               ery capacity. Although dietary fibre provides health benefits, excessive intake in female
1587	                               endurance athletes may have detrimental effects and therefore should be carefully managed
1588	                               when planning nutrition strategies [175]. A study of 364 endurance athletes identifying
1589	                               strategies used to alleviate exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms recommended
1590	                               pre-competition dietary modifications, such as reducing fibre and fat intake, adhering
1591	                               to a low fermentable oligosaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (FODMAP) diet,
1592	                               and implementing gut training. The most effective strategies for athletes were temporary
1593	                               fibre restriction, elimination of fermentable carbohydrates, and gradual adaptation of the
1594	                               gastrointestinal tract to carbohydrate intake during exercise. These practices are largely
1595	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                            33 of 43
1596	
1597	
1598	
1599	                               empirical and require further interventional studies for verification, highlighting the need
1600	                               for the development of standardised nutritional guidelines for endurance athletes [176,177].
1601	                                     In this review, studies were limited to molecular pathways, while mechanisms of
1602	                               the circadian clock or the detailed neuroendocrine effects of stress and neurotransmitters
1603	                               regulating sleep were not explored.
1604	                                     Significant challenges also arise in evaluating less tangible factors, such as psychologi-
1605	                               cal stress and mental load. Although these can be risk factors, their quantitative assessment
1606	                               remains difficult.
1607	                                     This review is constrained by the considerable heterogeneity of the included clinical
1608	                               studies. Participant characteristics varied widely in terms of age, sex, training status, and
1609	                               competitive level, ranging from recreationally active individuals to elite professional ath-
1610	                               letes. Sample sizes differed markedly between studies, from very small cohorts to larger
1611	                               observational groups, which complicates cross-study comparisons and limits the generaliz-
1612	                               ability of the findings. Additionally, study designs were diverse, including randomized
1613	                               controlled trials, crossover studies, prospective cohorts, and cross-sectional surveys, often
1614	                               with differing intervention protocols, outcome measures, and assessment tools. Such vari-
1615	                               ability reduces the ability to draw definitive conclusions regarding the effects of dietary
1616	                               factors on sleep in athletic populations. Furthermore, few studies investigated the interac-
1617	                               tions between meal timing, training intensity, and other environmental or lifestyle factors.
1618	                               Moreover, sleep measurement methods in sports research have limitations. Although
1619	                               ACG devices or screening questionnaires are often used, they are less accurate in assessing
1620	                               true sleep architecture and cannot replace the advantages of PSG. It is worth noting that
1621	                               these methods were not comprehensively reviewed, which may limit the interpretation
1622	                               of our findings [115]. Differences in metabolic demands and training loads across sports
1623	                               were not consistently considered, further limiting the applicability of results across athletic
1624	                               disciplines. These limitations underscore the need for more standardized, well-powered,
1625	                               and methodologically rigorous research in this field.
1626	                                     Finally, we highlight research directions and outline many questions regarding the
1627	                               impact of sport on sleep that require further verification and in-depth analysis. The lack
1628	                               of female participants in experimental studies and the limited experimental control in
1629	                               researching sleep in athletes remain gaps in the literature. There is also a need to validate
1630	                               and refine the tools used to assess sleep, ensuring they are suited to athletic populations.
1631	                               From a practical standpoint, future studies could examine the effects of napping and
1632	                               sleep extension (“banking sleep”) on performance [115], as well as the role of dietary
1633	                               interventions. Nutritional interventions can therefore modulate the sleep–wake cycle and
1634	                               are considered promising interventions, suggesting that further experiments in this area
1635	                               may yield new strategies to support athlete recovery.
1636	
1637	                               10. Summary
1638	                                    The management of sleep disturbances in athletes should prioritise non-pharmacological
1639	                               interventions, which have proven to be both effective and safe. These approaches, including
1640	                               cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), can significantly improve sleep quality,
1641	                               mental health, recovery, and athletic performance. While pharmacological treatment may
1642	                               be necessary in selected cases, it must be approached with caution, requiring not only
1643	                               medical expertise but also thorough consideration of anti-doping regulations and potential
1644	                               side effects. Consequently, pharmacological strategies should be reserved for situations
1645	                               in which behavioural interventions have failed, and only under the close supervision
1646	                               of qualified healthcare professionals. Ultimately, safeguarding the health and safety of
1647	                               the athlete, and upholding the integrity of competitive sport must remain central to all
1648	                               therapeutic decisions.
1649	 J. Clin. Med. 2025, 14, 7606                                                                                                     34 of 43
1650	
1651	
1652	
1653	                                     Treatment strategies should incorporate consistent lifestyle and environmental mod-
1654	                               ifications. Regular exposure to daylight, caffeine and alcohol restrictions, sleep hygiene
1655	                               optimisation, and the implementation of calming pre-sleep routines can enhance sleep
1656	                               quality and duration. Maintaining consistent sleep–wake schedules, integrating short
1657	                               restorative naps, and minimising evening exposure to electronic devices can also contribute
1658	                               to recovery. Team-based approaches, including routine assessment of sleep habits, travel
1659	                               schedules, and individualised sleep plans, are essential. Objective monitoring and early
1660	                               identification of disorders such as insomnia or obstructive sleep apnoea should form a core
1661	                               component of comprehensive athlete care (Figure 7).
1662	
1663	
1664	
1665	
1666	                               Figure 7. Summary of strategies for managing sleep disturbances in athletes. Created in BioRender.
1667	                               Kaczmarek, F. (2025) https://BioRender.com/vdb3yzg, (accessed on 20 October 2025).
1668	
1669	                               11. Conclusions
1670	                                     Optimal sleep duration and quality represent a critical “regenerative window”, essen-
1671	                               tial for enhancing athletic performance and safeguarding physiological resilience. Ensuring
1672	                               adequate sleep among athletes can be effectively achieved through the non-pharmacological
1673	                               interventions outlined in this review. This review uniquely substantiates this by examining
1674	                               the molecular consequences of sleep deprivation, such as the activation of pro-apoptotic
1675	                               gene pathways (BAX, CCAR2) and the disruption of circadian regulators (BMAL1). Further-
1676	                               more, the work presents a novel, practical analysis of pharmacological options, critically
1677	                               evaluating specific medications in the context of their impact on athletic performance and
1678	                               compliance with anti-doping regulations. Such an integrated approach, linking cellular
1679	                               mechanisms with clinical and nutritional strategies, provides a comprehensive understand-
1680	                               ing of how to optimise this critical regenerative window.
